en: Bestowing bliss upon living beings here by its own measure, and likewise in the hereafter through its nature as the Self of all, that state of Śaṅkarānanda which shines within the lotus of the heart—that is what ascetics enter. ||1||

This *Vivaraṇa*, an exposition upon the commentary (*bhāṣya*), together with a compendium of its underlying principles, is composed for the sake of abandoning the afflictions associated with the relationship between the explanation and that which is to be explained. (2)

Having studied the Vedānta according to the injunction for daily recitation, those qualified persons still have doubts regarding its meaning; [this work is intended] for them, as well as for those who rely on the Sūtras, the Bhāṣya, and other such texts. (3)

For the injunction for study is obligatory, according to the statement: "The Veda, along with its six auxiliary sciences, must be studied and understood as a duty without [extrinsic] motive by a Brāhmaṇa. If the study of the Veda were optional (kāmya), there would be a circular dependency: desire for understanding would arise once the meaning is known, and understanding of the meaning would occur once one has engaged in the study of the Veda equipped with its six auxiliaries due to that desire. Therefore, everyone studies the Veda together with its six auxiliaries and understands its meaning solely by the force of the obligatory injunction.

Someone, by virtue of the ripening of a mass of merit, seeking the unsurpassed goal of human life, searches for its means in the Veda and understands this: because of the statement that "everything becomes dear only for the sake of the Self," and because everything else is said to be dear only as subordinate to the Self, the qualified seeker is one who is detached from everything other than the Self; this is established by the opening statement, "Indeed, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known," and the concluding statement, "So much, my dear, is indeed immortality."

Having established that immortality—which constitutes the supreme human goal—is attained through the means of self-realization (*ātmadarśana*), and noting that such realization is not something subject to human volition and thus cannot be directly enjoined, the text reiterates the self-realization in the statement "The Self, indeed, is to be seen. It then prescribes *śravaṇa* (hearing) as the primary constituent (*aṅgin*) by means of the auxiliary constituents (*aṅga*) that assist toward the result—namely *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation)—in the injunction: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon. Thus, hearing is enjoined together with reflection and meditation as its subordinate factors.

If it is argued that even for one who has studied the Vedas along with their six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and understands the literal meaning of the Veda, the meaning understood by him cannot be what is intended by the scripture because the underlying intent (*tātparya*) is not grasped without inquiry, we say: not so; for it is precisely this intent of the scripture that is set forth in the Purāṇas. Thus it is said: "One should hear [the truth] from the sentences of the Vedas, and reflect upon it through logical reasonings.
Having known it, one should constantly meditate upon it; these are the means to realization. (1)

In this regard, O best of sages! "Hearing" (śravaṇa) consists merely in determining the power and intended meaning [of the scripture] by means of the indicators such as the introductory passages and so forth. (2)
From the mouth of the beloved teacher, one should receive all the Vedānta statements;
the practice of reasoning that supports those statements constitutes *manana* (reflection). || 3 ||
O wise ones! Both nididhyāsana—which is one-pointed concentration—and the pair consisting of hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana), are designated as nididhyāsana. 4.
O virtuous ones! Because it is an auxiliary factor that assists toward the fruit, such a misconception—though contrary to reality—is not without foundation, yet it perishes completely.

O wise ones! Because of the acts of reflecting (*manana*) upon it and also because of profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*), hearing (*śravaṇa*) is indeed the internal means for the arising of knowledge regarding this [Reality]. (6)
Likewise, reflection and contemplation are situated as bystanders through the exclusion of others;
and peace, self-control, and so forth, stand in the category of duties to be performed in due order. (7)

Then, for one whose mind is fixed upon all its constituent parts, there arises from the Vedic statements a pure mental modification (vṛtti) whose object is the identity of the inner self with Brahman. || 8 ||
In that [state], whatever manifestation of consciousness is self-established and belongs to Śaṅkara—that alone is the realization of Brahman; that alone is the destroyer of ignorance. (9)

That mental state which is of the nature of the identity between the inner self and Brahman arises as a full, extremely firm, and intense modification, produced by the causal complex characterized by the [great] word. 10.
And the inner self (pratyagātman), which is its witness, is self-luminous;
it is [conscious] solely by means of its own nature, which is Brahman.
O lords of sages! That ignorance, which is illuminated by consciousness, manifests itself within that [intellect] in the form of what is known as the knowledge of Brahman. 12.
Established solely through dependence, like the darkness of a bat, that which is unreal devours itself by its own nature according to the actual state of things. 13.
O wise ones! Having become serene in self, one’s own ignorance and its effects [vanish];
by means of one's own full Brahman-nature, one remains as oneself alone. 14.
O best of Brahmins, that by which such a remainder—which is the exclusive domain of one's own direct experience—is realized, is indeed the sovereign wisdom (vijñāna). || 15 ||

But even so, an injunction for hearing [the Vedānta] is not tenable. For instance: is it an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) like that for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice? Or is it an injunction of restriction (*niyama-vidhi*) like that for threshing and so forth? Or is it an injunction of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*) like "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten"? It cannot be the first, because the status of hearing the Vedānta and so forth as a means to the knowledge of Brahman—which is a perceptible result—is already established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For it is well known in the world that hearing the medical scriptures is a means for the comprehension of their subject matter. It is not the second [alternative], because there is no evidence to postulate a "restricted unseen merit" (*niyamādṛṣṭa*). In the case of threshing and the like, however, that which postulates such a thing is precisely the supreme *apūrva* produced by the restricted unseen merit. Furthermore, the knowledge of Brahman is not produced by an unseen merit, because there is an absence of negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*). Indeed, it has never been observed that even when the hearing of the Vedāntas and so forth are present, the knowledge of Brahman fails to arise due to the fault of an absence of restricted unseen merit.

Even if knowledge were somehow produced by an injunction (*vidhi*), this injunction would contradict the *Bhāṣya*; for in the commentary on the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, the injunction was refuted with great effort. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), whereby the Vedāntas would have both an injunction as their purport and Brahman as their purport. Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because—just as the eating of five-nailed or non-five-nailed animals is already established elsewhere so that one merely avoids the other—it is impossible for the direct realization of the Self (*ātma-sākṣātkāra*) to be obtained from anything other than the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, there is no injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*).

To this it is replied: Even in the case of the study of the Veda, which is a means for the knowledge of Dharma that yields a perceptible result, a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is indeed accepted. If such is the case even for the knowledge of Dharma—which is a human goal of limited scope and is indirect—then what need is there to mention that a restrictive injunction applies to *śravaṇa* (listening), which is a means for the direct realization of Brahman, the supreme human goal? If, in the case of study, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the restriction were the postulate for the sacrificial *apūrva*, then let the knowledge of Brahman itself be the postulate for the restriction in the case of *śravaṇa*.

This is because the knowledge of Brahman is produced by all unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), as the Smṛti states: "O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge. Here, the term "all" is used not to exclude well-known sacrifices and the like—which might lead one to mistakenly think that only those are intended—but rather to include even hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other such means; otherwise, there would be redundancy. As it is said: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself elsewhere, quickly becomes a Śūdra while still alive, along with his lineage."
If one accepts the existence of an injunction by considering the demerit incurred from its non-performance, then let it be the same in the present case as well:
"A renunciant who abandons his obligatory duties and lives without listening to the Vedānta certainly falls; of this there is no doubt."
This is because of the traditional teaching regarding the sin [of non-performance].

Now, one might object: since Brahman is devoid of attributes and is accessible through the Upanishads alone, there can be no establishment of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means as instruments for the knowledge of Brahman by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); so how can a restrictive rule (*niyama*) be established? Not so; just as in the injunction "one threshes the rice," even though threshing is not otherwise obtained for the rice intended for the unseen merit (*apūrva*) which is accessible solely through scripture, a restriction is nonetheless applied to threshing, so too let there be a restriction regarding hearing, even without its being merely optional.

Now, if it is argued that there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) with respect to the attainment [of rice] through the common form shared by all varieties of *vrīhi* grain, then this is the same in the present case as well, since it is easy to state a common form shared by all cognitions of the object.

Furthermore, if in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*), what is actually an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is conventionally designated as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) because of its result, then the same will apply to hearing (*śravaṇa*). Nor is there any contradiction with the Bhāṣya, for in that context, only the injunction to see (*darśana-vidhi*) is being rejected.

For if the injunction were directed toward "seeing" (darśana), then according to the grammatical maxim—"the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, with the suffix-meaning being predominant"—the injunction (*niyoga*), which is the meaning of the suffix, would be primary. Consequently, since "seeing" is subordinate as the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), Brahman, as its qualifier, would be even more subordinate. Therefore, Brahman would not be established by the Vedāntas. However, there is no such defect if the injunction of hearing (*śravaṇa*) is directed toward the "seeing of Brahman," which is the primary result.

And as for the charge of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), is it raised by the partisan (*ekadeśin*) or by the systematic scholar (*tāntrika*)? It cannot be the first, because even in the Vedānta, a syntactical split within a subordinate sentence is accepted, as in the passage "They desire to know through sacrifice," where sacrifices and other rites are admitted as means to knowledge. Nor can it be the second, for in the section on the *Pretāgnihotra*, after prescribing the holding of the fuel-stick below with the words "Holding the fuel-stick below, he should run after [the fire]," the text reads: "For he holds it above for the gods."

In this regard, the divine act of wearing [the sacred thread] over the shoulder, although heard within another context, must be understood as an injunction, because this was determined in the section titled "But there is an injunction regarding wearing, because it is something not previously established" (*vidhistu dhāraṇe 'pūrvatvāt*).

Now, even if Prabhākara were somehow unwilling to accept this particular section, he nevertheless accepts the injunction for a woman in her menses to perform a set of observances in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, namely: "She should observe the vow for three nights."

Therefore, let hearing (*śravaṇa*) be enjoined even within the context of Brahman; what loss is there for you? Now, if you argue that because the collection of observances cannot be connected to the context, one must resort to a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) out of necessity, whereas here it is not appropriate because the suffix *-tavya* can be construed even in the sense of "fitness" (*arha*), and thus you remain dissatisfied—then let the passage beginning with "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, having become learned... be the injunction for hearing and so forth; since that is studied outside of the initial commencement [of the Upaniṣads], there is no contradiction with what was stated.

Even if [the injunction] is not perceived upon the mere initial hearing, when the sentence is carefully examined, it is clear that the sentence’s primary intent is not an injunction for hearing and so forth; for the author of the Sūtras himself, in the sūtra "There is an injunction for another auxiliary" (*sahakāryantaravidhi*), having taken for granted the injunction of scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) and childhood (*bālya*) as consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), establishes in the subsequent phrase "then [he becomes] a sage" (*atha muniḥ*) that the state of being a sage (*mauna*) consists of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) and is thus enjoined. Therefore, the charge of being outside the traditional lineage (*asāmpradāyikatva*) is cast far away.

If it be objected that even so, the injunction to hear—that "it is to be heard"—which is already understood through the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), remains as inexplicable as before, we say no; for the suffix *-tavya* is remembered by grammatical tradition (*smṛti*) as being used even in the sense of an injunction. Furthermore, since in other scriptural passages belonging to the same context, such as "seek to know That" (*tadvijijñāsasva*), the injunction of hearing must necessarily be accepted as a separate syntactical unit (*vākyabheda*), there is no room for your dissatisfaction.

Nor should it be said that there is a redundant repetition of two injunctions regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*)—namely, "it is to be heard" and "having become learned"—within the very same branch [of the Veda], because in one place an injunction is laid down and in the other, having referred back to that [injunction], a specific detail is stated. Alternatively, just as the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is not redundant despite being repeated twice because one instance serves as a concluding summary, so too let there be a twofold injunction for hearing. Therefore, the injunction "it is to be heard" is indeed logically established. || 1 ||

In this context, "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) is defined by the statement of the Purāṇas: "It is the determination of the intended meaning of the Vedānta sentences by means of investigating them through such indicators as the opening statements (*upakrama*). Accordingly, one who is dispassionate and qualified for the inquiry must perform the investigation of the Vedānta sentences in order to attain the vision of the Self, which is the means to immortality.

Thus, a person who has studied the Veda, having first understood [the truth] from the Veda itself, subsequently reflects as follows: "Is mere detachment (*vairāgya*) alone the qualification for eligibility, or is there something else as well? What is the authority regarding these various qualifications and the qualified candidate endowed with them? Has the inquiry into the Vedānta texts already been accomplished by the inquiry into *dharma*, or not? How are the Vedānta texts to be investigated? What is the defining characteristic of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), and what is the authority regarding it? And is that authority [established] by anyone..."

Is there no contradiction? Furthermore, does knowledge whose object is reality lead to immortality when combined with ritual actions, or is it the sole means? If it is the sole means, what is the proof for that? And of what nature is this immortality, and what is its authority? These doubts, as well as others of a similar kind, must be resolved through various lines of reasoning.

And the most compassionate Lord Bādarāyaṇa, desiring to set forth those principles in aphoristic form (*sūtra*), first established—by means of logical reasoning—the injunction contained in the statement "It is to be heard," which is endowed with the three subordinate elements (*anubandha*) known as the qualified person, the subject matter, and the fruit; and he then aphorized the necessity of the inquiry into that [injunction's] meaning as the introductory premise (*upodghāta*) for the commencement of the entire forthcoming treatise: "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).

In that regard, the very person who is understood to be qualified by the sentence "But for the sake of one's own desires"—namely, one endowed with the fourfold means characterized by dispassion—is precisely the meaning of the word *atha*. Furthermore, in the statement "But there is no hope for immortality through wealth," it is said that immortality cannot be attained through worldly and Vedic rituals characterized by wealth; this very point is made the reason by the word *ataḥ*.

By the sentence beginning with "Indeed, in the self," it has been stated that one must perform *śravaṇa*—which consists of the inquiry into the Vedānta texts—for the sake of attaining the vision of the Self, which is the means to immortality. All of that is to be understood by the term *brahmajijñāsā*.

Now, is this aphorism injunctive or reiterative? It cannot be the first, because no optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), or gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes are observed. Nor can it be the latter, for if it were not injunctive, there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to include the injunction to hear the scripture. This is not so; for the word "to be performed" (*kartavyā*) is to be supplied by ellipsis. If it is argued that since knowledge and desire depend on the nature of the object and cannot be brought about by human effort, the term *jijñāsā* (desire to know) would not connect with the supplied word, then—precisely because of this incongruity—the term *jijñāsā* must be taken as indicating, through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the inquiry (*vicāra*) which is fit to be undertaken.

Furthermore, the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is easily established through the logic of the "tongs" (*sandaṃśanyāya*). For inquiry is gripped by both knowledge and desire; for when desire exists first, inquiry follows, and only subsequently does knowledge arise. Nor should it be argued that, in the case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), only the connection with the subject matter called "inquiry" would be established, and not the connection with the result called "knowledge of Brahman," because even the primary meaning is accepted through "non-abandoning indication" (*ajahallakṣaṇā*).

The fact that the Vedāntic texts are the subject matter of inquiry is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for their capacity to generate knowledge of Brahman; indeed, we do not observe the knowledge of Brahman arising in those who investigate other subjects. Furthermore, the status of the knowledge of Brahman as a means to liberation is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its being a fruit; for a "fruit" is that which is desired by qualified aspirants. In this context, qualified aspirants—endowed with the fourfold prerequisites—desire nothing other than the total eradication of suffering, the attainment of unsurpassed bliss, and the means thereto.

Since it is impossible for the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) to consist in the destruction of suffering and the attainment of bliss [in itself], it follows by process of elimination that it is the means to those ends.

Thus, the entire meaning of the Śruti—that one endowed with the fourfold qualifications must undertake an inquiry into the Vedānta texts for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation, since liberation cannot be achieved through ritual actions—is summarized in this Sūtra.

Thus, the fact that the commencement of the treatise is caused by the necessity of inquiry is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For when there is an injunction endowed with the three prerequisites (*anubandha-traya*), persons engage in action, as is observed in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others. But when such an injunction is absent, they do not engage; for instance, no engagement is observed regarding statements such as "The earth consists of seven islands. And that necessity of inquiry—which serves as the cause for the commencement of the treatise to be explained—is determined in this manner by the present first Sūtra: [The Sūtra: *Athāto brahmajijñāsā*. (Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. [Commentary: Here, the word *atha* ("now") signifies immediate succession (*anantarya*) and not a new beginning (*ārambha*). This is because it is impossible for the commencement of the inquiry to depend on anything other than the completion of its prerequisite. Furthermore, since the completion of the prerequisite is understood from the very word *atha*, there is no need to assume another meaning for it. Moreover, since the word *atha* is conventionally used to denote immediate succession—as in "Now he eats"—its primary meaning is indeed immediate succession. It cannot be taken in a secondary sense, for there is no reason to set aside its primary meaning. Nor can it be argued that the primary meaning is impossible here; for the completion of the prerequisite is possible, namely, the completion of the qualification (*adhikāra*) consisting in the possession of the four means [discrimination, dispassion, concentration, and the desire to know], which is the cause of the inquiry. The word *ataḥ* ("therefore") denotes cause (*hetu*). It indicates that the inquiry into Brahman follows immediately after the completion of the aforementioned qualification. The compound *brahmajijñāsā* is a genitive-tatpuruṣa, meaning "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇo jijñāsā*). Since the genitive case is used in a non-possessive sense, it expresses the object of the desire. Thus, the meaning is: "The desire to know has Brahman as its object. What is this Brahman? It is that whose nature is defined by the attributes of eternity, purity, consciousness, and freedom, and which is indicated by the term "That" (*tat*) in the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*): "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). What is the purpose of this inquiry? It is the attainment of the supreme human goal, which is the direct realization of that very Brahman. What is the connection between the inquiry and the purpose? It is the relationship of means and end (*sādhya-sādhana-bhāva*). Thus, the necessity of the inquiry is established by this Sūtra as being the cause for the commencement of the treatise described above. This is because, when the injunction is thus characterized by the three prerequisites, people engage in action, as seen in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth; whereas in its absence they do not, as seen in the lack of engagement with statements like "The earth consists of seven islands. And this necessity of inquiry, which is the cause for the commencement of the treatise to be explained, is determined in this manner by the present first Sūtra.

This treatise ought to be commenced, because it possesses a probable subject matter and purpose, just like agriculture and other such activities. Nor should it be suspected that this subject matter is not established by the Sūtra on the grounds that the subject and purpose are not explicitly mentioned therein; for even if they are not stated directly, they are indicated by implication. Indeed, such indication is an ornament of a Sūtra, not a defect.

In this regard, first of all, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the Vedānta texts—which are to be investigated by means of the scripture beginning with "From which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this [world]"—is the identity of Brahman and the Self, as established by such scriptural passages as "That indeed is this Self; It is Brahman. And that identity has been indicated in the aphorism by the word *brahman*, which denotes an entity that is undivided and of a single essence. The purpose (*prayojana*) is the cessation of suffering and the attainment of Brahman, as established by such scriptural passages as "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow" and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

And these two have indeed been indicated by the mention of the knowledge of Brahman, which serves as their means of accomplishment. Not only did the author of the Sūtras indicate the subject matter and the purpose, but he also intended to establish them in this manner: "The scripture under discussion possesses a possible subject matter and purpose, because it is the antidote to bondage consisting of nescience, just like waking consciousness."

Nor should it be said that the fact that bondage consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not indicated by the Sūtra; for that is indeed indicated simply by the acceptance that bondage is removable by knowledge (*jñāna*). To explain: the author of the Sūtras has accepted that the removal of all suffering constitutes the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman in order to establish its status as a result. Furthermore, all forms of bondage—such as being a knower (*pramātṛ*), an agent (*kartṛ*), and an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)—are nothing but suffering, since they are the seeds of suffering.

In this regard, it must be investigated: is this bondage real (pāramārthika) or unreal (apāramārthika)? If it were the former, it could not be removed by the knowledge of Brahman. Those partial theorists (ekadeśins) and others who maintain that even a real bondage is removed by knowledge should be asked: does knowledge produce an excellence called "cessation" either in its own object or in its own substrate? If the former, does it remove the transmigrating self (saṃsārin) which is the very object of that knowledge, or merely the attributes (dharma) residing therein, or else...?

Do [these cognitions] remove agency and so forth—which are opposed to non-existence—by means of their own indivisible cognitions of the object, or rather do they remove only the lack of cognition regarding the object itself? It cannot be the first, second, or third [options], for the cognition of the blue portion in a multi-colored fruit such as a mango does not remove its own object, nor the yellow color and other qualities inherent in it, which are its opposites. In the fourth case, however, there is the consequence of adopting our own position.

Even regarding the position that [bondage] is an excellence of the substratum (*āśrayātiśaya*), does it consist in the cessation of the substratum itself, or of its qualities, or of those properties related to both the substratum and its object? Not the first, because it would entail the destruction of the self at every moment. Not the second, because the knowledge of a pot does not cause the cessation of the qualities such as the properties residing in the self. Not the third, because the knowledge of one's own body does not cause the cessation of the relationship between the body and the self, and so forth. If it is argued that even real bondage is removed by knowledge, on the basis of the scriptural text, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," we say no.

Because the scripture maintains neutrality regarding whether bondage is real or unreal; rather, we postulate the non-existence of bondage for the sake of making the scripture logically consistent. This is just as you postulate the *apūrva* (unseen potency) for the sake of making the scriptural statement that the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices are means to attaining heaven logically consistent.

Now, if it is argued that in that case there exists a restrictive rule of pervasion (*vyāpti-niyama*)—namely, that momentary actions lack the capacity to produce results occurring at a later time—then here too, let there be a restrictive rule of pervasion: "Knowledge alone is the remover of ignorance. Consequently, the non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*) of bondage remains established. Thus, the fact that bondage—which is removable by the knowledge of Brahman—is of the nature of ignorance is indicated by the Sūtra itself.

[Objection: In that case, the fact that [the world] consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) should have been described by the author of the Sūtras explicitly, because this serves to establish the commencement of the entire treatise by way of its subject matter, purpose, and proof. If you argue that failing to state it explicitly would result in the charge of a lack of intent (*atātparya*), then this has indeed already been stated explicitly in the second chapter in the Sūtra beginning with "Because its essence consists of those qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*).

And this is the meaning of the Sūtra: if it is argued that the omnipresence of the Self is contradicted by the scriptural accounts of its departure from the body, its transition to the next world, and its return to this world, [the answer is] because the intellect (*buddhi*) is its essence. Due to the mutual superimposition of identity between the intellect and the Self, there arises in the omnipresent Self a mere conceit regarding the qualities of the intellect, such as departure and so forth. And this [conceit] is restated by the Scripture for the purpose of revealing its own true nature.

If it is argued that, because it serves as an introductory prelude (*upodghāta*) to the commencement of the entire treatise, the sūtra concerning superimposition (*adhyāsa*) should have been composed at the very beginning, and that an introductory prelude consists of the description of another matter prior to the subject to be established having been grasped by the intellect—this is not so; for the author of the sūtras, being engaged in the task of establishing his own position, would be unable to state the sūtra intended to resolve contradictions at the outset.

"Establishment" (*pratipādana*) consists in first stating the subject to be established (*pratipādya*) explicitly as a proposition (*pratijñā*), and subsequently demonstrating the reasons for its proof. Accordingly, having demonstrated the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts with Brahman in the first chapter, the resolution of contradictions that serves to establish it must be undertaken afterwards. Otherwise, if the specific concordance were not first demonstrated, any suspicion of contradiction and its subsequent refutation would be rendered objectless.

[Objection: "But if superimposition (adhyāsa) were not mentioned at the very beginning, the subject matter and the purpose would not be established, and consequently, the engagement with this treatise would not occur. [Reply: Not so; for it has already been demonstrated that although superimposition is not explicitly stated in the first aphorism, it is nonetheless indicated by implication, and thus the engagement with the treatise is indeed established.

But surely, even though superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is indicated by the Sūtra, it cannot withstand logical scrutiny. For instance: the Self and the non-Self are devoid of mutual superimposition of identity, because they are devoid of mutual existence in any case, like darkness and light. Nor is the reason unestablished: the two subjects under dispute are devoid of identity, because they possess contradictory natures, like darkness and light. Nor is the reason unestablished: the two subjects under dispute possess contradictory natures, because they are the objects of the "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "I" (*asmat*) cognitions, like Devadatta and his enemy.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of Devadatta’s own body and its aggregates there is the notion of "I," while in those very same things belonging to his enemy there is the notion of "you," and yet no contradiction exists therein; for if one were to apply this by transposing the notions even to the enemy’s case, the illustrative example would be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). For we do not intend the objects of two notions residing in different substrata to be the example; rather, we intend those residing in the same substratum. Nor do we intend the mere forms of the cognizers themselves to be the example.

What then? The example is the form of the aggregate established through the cognition of Devadatta and the cognition of his enemy; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. It might be argued: "In this context, are the self and the non-self taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) according to worldly consensus, or according to the systems of the Prābhākaras and others, or according to the Vedāntins? Not the first, because both of the two inferences would suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). Nor the third, because that inference contradicts experience. For in the world, the 'self' is the aggregate beginning with the body and ending with consciousness, while the 'non-self' consists of stones and the like."

Nor is there, as the Vedāntins maintain, an identification through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) between the two; nor is an absolute contradiction between them perceived. It is not the second [alternative] either, for the Prābhākaras and others assert that the Self is insentient (*jaḍa*), being the locus of the states of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*), agent (*kartṛtva*), and enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), while they regard the entire phenomenal world—including the senses, the body, and so forth—as non-Self (*anātman*). In that case, according to the Vedāntic view, both the locus of the states of being a knower and the insentience that causes it—namely, ignorance (*ajñāna*)—would reside solely in the non-Self, which is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

Furthermore, since it is not accepted that there can be a superimposition of identity between the non-self and a single category [of the self], the two previously mentioned defects would necessarily follow. It cannot be the third [alternative], for the Vedāntins maintain that the Self is a mass of consciousness devoid of all attributes, and everything other than that is the non-self. In this regard, is it intended as a reason that both cognitions have a single object, or that the Self is the object of the "I-notion" while the non-self is the object of the other? In the first case, there is the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*); in the second, there is the fallacy of partial unestablishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*).

If it is argued that because the notion of "thou" (*yuṣmat-pratyaya*) does not arise with respect to the body, senses, internal organ, vital breath, and so forth—which are non-self—there is indeed the notion of "thou" there according to the definition "the object of 'thou' is that which is illumined by consciousness," even though such a notion is absent from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra-dṛṣṭi*), yet present from the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstra-d�̣ṛṣṭi*); even so, that defect remains as it was, because for the Vedāntins, the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*) does not arise with respect to the self-luminous conscious Self (*cid-ātman*). Therefore, the [self] is not established through inference.

To this it is replied: for the Vedāntin, the establishment of inference certainly exists. Nor is there a partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*) with respect to the Self; for even though the Self is self-luminous, its being the object of the notion "I" (*asmat-pratyaya-gocaratva*) can be figuratively attributed to the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) by virtue of its being clearly fit for such linguistic usage. Nor should it be thought that the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because there is no contradiction between two consciousnesses—the witnesses of the two bodies—even if they stand respectively as the referents of "you" (*yuṣmad-artha*) and "I" (*asmad-artha*).

Because consciousness lacks the status of being the object of "you" (yuṣmad-artha), as characterized by the definition of being illumined by consciousness; and it is precisely such [consciousness] that is intended here, not the worldly referent of "you. If it is argued that, nevertheless, contradiction is established through this inference by way of the cognition and not by its own nature, then let it be so.

Self and non-self possess contradictory natures, because they stand in the relation of subject and object, like the eye and form. Now, if it is argued: "The conscious self is experienced as being favorable toward the unconscious non-self by acting as its means of realization; therefore, there is a contradiction with experience in establishing a hostility characterized either by the relation of slayer and slain, or by the incapacity for coexistence; likewise, the illustrative example is deficient in the property to be proven," we say: not so.

This is because, in this context, what is intended by "contradiction" (*virodha*) is characterized by the absence of the capacity for mutual identity, as in the case of existence and non-existence. If it is asked, "How then can darkness and light serve as an example in the middle inference, since their contradiction is well-known as being characterized by the absence of the capacity for coexistence?"—it is not so; for in a room with a dim lamp, darkness coexists with the light. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one could perceive forms clearly here as well, just as in a place of intense illumination.

If it is argued that by the words "darkness" (tamas) and "light" (prakāśa), their constituent parts—shadow (chāyā) and sunlight (ātapa)—are indicated, even so, the heat perceived in a single instance of shadow necessarily indicates the presence of its own substratum, the sunlight; thus, their co-existence remains unavoidable.

In the same way, even if one accepts coldness and heat as residing in shadow and sunlight through the secondary metaphorical indication (*lakṣita-lakṣaṇā*) of the terms "darkness" and "light," their coexistence is easily established. Therefore, the very fact that the capacity for identity exists between a genus and an individual, but not so between darkness and light, is precisely what constitutes their opposition.

If it is argued that in the analogy of darkness and light, the property of being a positive entity (*bhāva*) rather than a non-entity (*abhāva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*), such that the Naiyāyikas hold "darkness is the absence of light" and the Prābhākaras hold "darkness is the absence of the perception of color"—this is not so. For that which is perceived as possessing various states such as increase and decrease cannot logically be a non-entity. Furthermore, because it possesses the quality of blue color, it must be a substance (*dravya*). If it is asked: "In the view that darkness is a positive entity, how can one with closed eyes perceive darkness in a place filled with intense light, given that you admit [in that case] that darkness is removed by the intense light?"

If it is argued that coexistence with the light of the eye was already stated previously, we say no; for the perception of darkness existing within the eyeball is logically established. Nor is it impossible for the eye to grasp an object situated inside it, since we observe that one who has closed their ears perceives internal sounds. Furthermore, this does not entail the undesirable consequence of being able to perceive collyrium and the like located inside the eyeball when the eyes are closed; because there is a rule that only material objects other than darkness, which possess color-form (*rūpin*), are perceptible by the eye when assisted by light.

Now, if it is thought that, while darkness is a substance, there is no immediate production of it upon the removal of light once it has been destroyed by light—because effect-substances are produced only through the sequence of dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth—that is not so; for those who maintain the doctrine of illusory manifestation (vivartavādins), no such sequence is required, as the cause is indeed primordial ignorance (mūlāvidyā). If it is argued that darkness is not a substance possessing color because it is devoid of touch, like space, we say no; for this is equivalent to the fallacious argument: "Air is not tangible because it is devoid of color, like space," since the contradiction with perception is equal in both cases.

Now, if it is argued that the perception of darkness has a different explanation—namely, that it perceives a superimposed blue color in the absence of light—even so, the reason remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For smoke, which is a substance possessing color, lacks touch in locations other than where it is seen by the eye. If it is argued that the touch of smoke exists there but is merely unmanifest (*anudbhūta*), then the touch of darkness must likewise exist everywhere but be unmanifest; thus, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, it is not impossible for that which exists to fail to manifest everywhere; for we observe that in gold and other minerals produced from mines, although they possess a luminous form that illuminates both itself and others, as well as a hot touch, these qualities do not manifest everywhere. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the doctrine that darkness is a positive entity (bhāva). If it is argued that the same applies to the doctrine of non-existence (abhāva)—since states such as increase and so forth are conditioned by their counter-correlate (pratiyogin), namely light, and since the blue color [of darkness] is merely superimposed—this is not so, because it is difficult to define. To explain: is darkness the absence of light in general, the absence of each individual light, or the absence of all lights?

In the first and second positions, it is difficult to maintain that darkness is prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), or destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); for there is no cognition of darkness in a place permeated by the rays of the sun, whether before a lamp has been lit, once the lamp has been lit, or when the lamp has been extinguished. In the third position, [the cognition of darkness] would not cease except in the presence of all light.

It is also incorrect to claim that darkness is the absence of the perception of form, because for one situated in the middle of a room shrouded in dense darkness, both the perception of external forms and the perception of [the internal] darkness occur simultaneously. Therefore, darkness is not an absence; thus, the aforementioned limiting condition (upādhi) does not exist in the illustrative example.

[Objection: Even so, your fundamental reason—namely, "the absence of the capacity for mutual identity"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For in the case of an error such as "this is silver," even though there is an absence of the capacity for identity between the distinct objects—the object in front and the silver—an identity is nevertheless perceived. [Response: No; because in that case, the reason does not apply, since the capacity for identity actually exists there.

And it should not be argued that the reason (*hetu*) [of the argument] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because its capacity is possible given a real identity (*tādātmya*) between the silver and the object standing before one in the locus of the "real" (*samyag-rajata-sthala*); for such a real identity between these two can never be established. To explain: is it the identity of the seer with the seen that is asserted, or the identity of the seen with the seer? In the first case as well, it cannot be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), because the aspect of the seen is impossible within the seer, who consists solely of consciousness (*cidekarasa*).

Otherwise, identity would be untenable due to the relationship between the object and the agent of action (*karmakartṛbhāva*). Even if [the seer] were adventitious (*āgantuka*), would it assume the form of the visible portion by its own nature or through the power of a cause? Both are inconsistent, because the seer is partless (*niravayava*). Indeed, space, being partless, is never seen to transform into a form possessing parts, either inherently or through another cause. Furthermore, in the second position—that the seer is identical with the visible subject (*dharmin*) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—if the state of being a seer were intrinsic, the state of being visible would be lost.

If it is argued that even a portion of itself is visible, then there is the contradiction of being both object and agent. Even if this visibility is adventitious, does the visible object transform itself into the nature of consciousness, or does it transfer the consciousness of the Self into itself? It cannot be the first, because it is impossible for an effect produced from an insentient cause to possess the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa); for a jar, which is a transformation of insentient clay, is never seen to be of the nature of consciousness. Nor can it be the second; for the consciousness of the Self, being omnipresent, cannot actually enter [into another] in reality.

Thus, since it is impossible for consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*)—which possess an essential identity that is in some cases extremely difficult to establish—to possess such causal capacity, the middle inference is well-established as proving the reason. Consequently, the primary inference is established, and the non-existence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is firmly settled.

"Let it be that there is no superimposition of identity between the two substrates; nevertheless, let there be a superimposition of the attributes of the Self upon the non-Self through their association. Nor is it impossible for the Self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, to possess attributes, since bliss, the experience of objects, eternality, and so forth do exist. Although these are indeed the very essence of the Self, they appear as if manifold due to the limiting adjunct of the modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti); thus, their status as 'attributes' is used figuratively."

Nor is it impossible for attributes (*dharma*) to be superimposed independently of their substratum (*dharmin*), since we observe the superimposition of mere attributes in cases such as "the crystal is red" when in proximity to a hibiscus flower. This is not sound, because attributes cannot exist independently. Even in the case of the crystal, the redness perceived is dependent solely upon the reflected hibiscus flower, and not independently. Therefore, there is no superimposition of relation (*saṃsargādhyāsa*) among attributes through a transposition of their substrata.

Since the superimposition of the two objects—the property and the substratum—has been refuted, the superimposition of cognition, which is invariably concomitant with them, is likewise refuted. Therefore, superimposition is not tenable when subjected to logical analysis.

To this it is replied: Is the unreality of superimposition (adhyāsa) being established here because of its contradiction with reason, or is its very nature as a real entity being denied? It is not the first; for us, who maintain the doctrine of indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva), both the unreality of superimposition and its contradiction with reason are accepted. Indeed, it is precisely because that superimposition of Self and non-Self is contradicted by reason that its indeterminability is admitted. Otherwise, one would have to accept its status as a real entity.

[Objection: In that case, we shall simply deny superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—that is, there is no superimposition of the self upon the non-self at all, because its causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) are absent. For in the world, in instances such as "this is silver" or "this is a snake," the causal condition for superimposition is a similarity between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object superimposed (*adhyasyamāna*) produced by qualities or parts; and that [similarity] does not exist here, because the Self is devoid of qualities and devoid of parts. Nor should it be argued that superimposition occurs even when the aforementioned similarity is absent, as in the case of "the crystal is red."

In that case, because it is an error conditioned by an external adjunct (*sopādhika-bhrama*), there is no dependence on similarity; for the proximate hibiscus flower, which is the locus of the redness, serves as the adjunct, since it is the cause for the appearance of redness in the crystal.

If it is argued that, in this way, by taking the ego (ahaṅkāra)—which is in close proximity and serves as the substratum for agency and so forth—as an adjunct (upādhi), it is possible to superimpose agency and other such qualities upon the Self, then let it be granted that the superimposition of agency and so forth may somehow be possible; nevertheless, the superimposition of the attributes of the ego up to the body upon the Self cannot possibly occur without an adjunct, because of the absence of similarity. To this, we reply: this argument is unsubstantial.

Just as even for fragrance—which is devoid of both qualities (*guṇa*) and constituent parts (*avayava*)—there is a similarity by way of the property of "sweetness" (as in "the smell of a snake is similar to the smell of a *ketakī* flower"), so too a similarity of the self is possible by way of the property of "being a category" (*padārthatva*). If it is argued that no property whatsoever is actually possible in that which has the singular essence of pure consciousness, then let there be no causal efficacy of similarity with respect to a cognition that is free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhika-bhrama*).

For even in the absence of similarity, we observe unconditioned errors such as "the conch is yellow. Now, if you argue that in that case there exists another causal complex consisting of the excess of bile, jaundice, cataracts, and so forth, then indeed there exists here too a causal complex known as ignorance (*avidyā*).

If it is argued that since ignorance (*avidyā*)—which is disputed as being both an absence of knowledge and a positive entity—is accepted as the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it would be better simply to deny superimposition (*adhyāsa*) altogether, we say: not so. For it is impossible to deny that beginningless, perceptible [ignorance] which exists as the veiler of the consciousness and bliss of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), depending solely upon the existence of that very self. Otherwise, the inner self itself would have to be denied.

If it is argued that it is illogical for the effect, which is superimposition (*adhyāsa*), to be beginningless, we say: not so. First, in the case of the Self, superimposition is precisely the conjunction with defects such as agency, enjoyership, and passion. Among these, the superimposition of enjoyership depends upon the superimposition of agency, because there is no enjoyment for one who is not an agent. Furthermore, agency depends upon the superimposition of the conjunction with defects such as passion, because one devoid of passion and the like lacks agency. And the conjunction with defects depends upon enjoyership, because passion and the like do not arise in one who has not experienced [an object] or in one belonging to a class that has not experienced it.

And thus, like the seed and the sprout, agency and the rest are beginningless by way of a continuous stream. By this, the following objection is also refuted: that there is mutual dependence, such that the superimposition occurs when the world-appearance is perceived, and the perception occurs when there is superimposition. For, given their beginninglessness, the body and so forth—manifested by each preceding superimposition and persisting in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—serve as the cause for each subsequent superimposition.

Nor should it be argued that because the body and so forth are unreal, there can be no superimposition [upon them]; for once it is established that something is an object of superimposition by mere cognition, the actual existence of the thing is irrelevant as a factor. For in cases such as "this is silver," the identity between the real and the unreal—the mother-of-pearl and the silver—is superimposed. Nor should it be argued that in the case of two trees standing at a distance, it is the identity of two things that are both real which is being superimposed; even there, while the substratum consists of two real trees, it is precisely an unreal attribute—namely, oneness—that is superimposed. Otherwise, it would follow that even the identity between two real entities, such as a quality and its possessor, must be considered a superimposition.

Although the mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the Self and the non-Self upon each other is the same in that they are not identical with one another, nevertheless, the Self possesses reality because its superimposition occurs only in its associated form and not in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); whereas the non-Self possesses unreality because its superimposition occurs even in its own essential nature.

Furthermore, if there were identity between those two—the real and the unreal—there would not arise a cognition such as "I possess a body and senses" or "this body and so forth belong to me," based on the appearance of both difference and non-difference (as in the case of a quality and its possessor, e.g., "the cloth is white"). This is because superimposition is accepted only after establishing a state of absolute oneness between the two. If it is argued that one should therefore not say "superimposition of identity" but rather "superimposition of oneness," we reply: no.

This is because we observe the usage of difference in expressions such as "my body," just as one says "the whiteness of the cloth. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, since the apprehension of difference—which is the pervader—has ceased, superimposition (adhyāsa), which is its pervaded, must also cease; for we do not admit the apprehension of difference [in this context]. Indeed, ordinary people, while using the expression "my body" and thus dealing with difference, do not—without the refinement provided by the scriptures—apprehend the Self as distinct from the body.

Therefore, from the perspective of direct experience (*anubhava*), it can be designated as the superimposition of identity (*ekatvādhyāsa*) alone, whereas from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), it can also be designated as the superimposition of oneness (*tādātmyādhyāsa*). This is because there exists both the empirical usage of non-difference in the form "I am the body" (*ahaṃ dehaḥ*) and the empirical usage of difference in the form "this is my body" (*mama dehaḥ*). Nor should it be said that identity is nothing other than oneness; for identity is that which is compatible with both difference and non-difference and is opposed to mutual negation (*anyonyābhāva*), whereas oneness is opposed to difference—thus the two are distinct.

Even in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, their identity is designated as "oneness" in reality, while their "selfhood" (*tādātmya*) is spoken of with reference to the difference imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the identity of the self and the body, though experienced like that of the soul and Brahman, cannot be real; for since the two are utterly distinct by nature—as truth and untruth—actual identity is impossible. Therefore, their oneness is merely superimposed (*adhyasta*).

And the material cause (*upādāna*) of that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*); for when this [ignorance] exists, superimposition arises, and when it is absent, it does not arise. If it is argued that these two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—are also accounted for by taking the absence of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which acts as an obstacle to superimposition, as the object [of the relationship], we say no; because the knowledge of reality lacks the defining characteristic of being an obstacle. Indeed, the knowledge of reality arises even while the abundant causes of superimposition—namely, defects such as cataracts and jaundice—still exist; thus, it is devoid of the characteristic [of being an obstacle].

If it is argued that, nevertheless, since the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is opposed to superimposition (*adhyāsa*), those two [non-existences] may be established as having the absence of a contrary connection as their object, we say no. For an effect first requires its material cause (*upādāna*), and only subsequently does it require the absence of a contrary connection. Thus, according to the maxim "between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger," it is logical that those two have the internal material cause as their object. If it is argued that, like destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), they might simply not require a material cause at all;

The subject under dispute possesses an *upādāna* (material cause), because, while being an entity, it is an effect, like a jar—this is the inference. Now, an objection is raised: the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the quality of color (*rūpa*) in a cloth, for that [color] cannot have an *upādāna*. Does that [color] have the cloth itself as its *upādāna*, or another substance? It cannot be the first, because a causal relationship is impossible between two things produced simultaneously, such as the left and right horns of a cow. In the second case, since it would reside in a different substance, its status as a quality of the cloth would be lost. To this we reply: not so.

First, according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), by the principle that "a substance, once produced, remains for a moment without qualities," there is an absence of simultaneity; thus, it is possible for the cloth itself to be the material cause (*upādāna*). However, in the Vedāntic view, even though the threads are the material cause, because of the non-difference between cause and effect, the quality of being a property of the cloth is not lost. Nor should it be argued: "Even if defects such as glass could possibly be material causes, what is the use of this *ajñāna*? For there is a rule that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and its material cause must have the same locus.

In this case, however, since the superimposition (adhyāsa) resides in the Self and the defects reside in the sense organs and so forth, they cannot be the material cause (upādāna). Now, one might object: "In your own view as well, the superimposition of silver is perceived as residing in the mother-of-pearl, whereas its material cause—ignorance (ajñāna)—resides in the Self; thus, even for you, the identity of locus is not established. This is not so; for we shall demonstrate that it is precisely the superimposition residing in the Self that has a connection with the mother-of-pearl.

If it is argued that, in that case, let ignorance (*ajñāna*) be the material cause (*upādāna*) for the superimposition of objects, while for the superimposition of cognitions, both the Self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) shall be the material causes—since they are found to be the material causes of correct cognitions according to different philosophical views—we say: not so; because the Self is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*), and because the internal organ depends upon the contact of the senses, inferential signs (*liṅga*), and so forth. For such contact and the like are not possible here [in the case of erroneous cognition].

Since a false object, whose body consists merely of cognition, is not established prior to that cognition, with what could the sense organ come into contact? Furthermore, the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the sense organs is otherwise accounted for as being directed toward the locus of the erroneous cognition.

Nor is the production of erroneous cognition established merely through association with the substrate (the knowledge of the locus), because such a cognition would be impossible in the absence of association with a false object. Nor is the cognition of thatness [in the recognition "This is that Devadatta"] comparable to the recognition itself, as it is brought forth by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); for, like that recognition, it would then result in being non-erroneous. Nor can its erroneous nature be due to the non-existence of the aspect consisting of the substrate’s connection [with the superimposed];
for, since that [connection] is non-existent and thus unfit for sensory contact, it would follow that the superimposed object—which lacks direct perception—could not appear as immediate (*aparokṣa*).

If it is argued that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) does not depend on contact with the sense organs regarding false objects, since dream-cognition is observed even without such contact; even so, because the internal organ lacks the nature of a knower during its transformation into the form of cognition, the empirical usage of false objects would not be established. Or, if you should think that the internal organ itself, though insentient, will transform into the form of being the agent of cognition, or that the Self will be the knower; [we reply:]...

Even so, since it is a necessary rule that error, right vision, and the cessation of bondage must have a single locus, if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were the locus of error, then right vision and the cessation of bondage would necessarily belong to that very same organ. However, it is accepted that error and the rest belong to the Self (*ātman*) alone; and this is established only on the view that ignorance (*ajñāna*), which has the Self as its locus, is the material cause (*upādāna*), and not otherwise. Therefore, ignorance alone remains as the material cause.

Nor should one dispute regarding ignorance (*ajñāna*); for the inert power of nescience (*avidyā-śakti*), which rests upon the Self and pervades both external and internal objects, is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the form: "I am ignorant" and "I do not know myself or another. Now, if it is argued that this experience has as its object the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), that is not so; for, like the experience "I am happy," it is an immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*). Furthermore, absence is cognizable only through the sixth means of valid knowledge (*ṣaṣṭha-pramāṇa*).

In the theory that the non-existence [of knowledge] is perceived directly (*pratyakṣābhāvavāda*), however, if both the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—namely, the self and the cognition—are perceived, then a direct perception of the absence of knowledge such as "there is no knowledge in me" would be contradicted. If, on the other hand, those two are not perceived, then the direct perception of that [absence] does not arise precisely because of the absence of its cause. If it is argued that in all cases practical activity (*vyavahāra*) serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for cognition, and thus the absence of cognition is inferred from the absence of that mark, we say no; for even then, the aforementioned defects regarding the perception or non-perception of the substratum and so forth remain.

Even in the Bhaṭṭa school’s view that the sixth [means of knowledge] is the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*), this same defect remains. In our view, however, the mere absence of cognition is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*). But the absence of a specific cognition is accessible through the sixth means of knowledge, according to the acceptance of the principle: "In worldly practice, the Bhaṭṭa position prevails. However, when one does not accept the category of non-existence (*abhāva*) at all, following the Purāṇic doctrine that "the earth becomes a jar, from a jar come potsherds, from potsherds powder-dust, and from that an atom," then there is no concern whatsoever.

Objection: Since even ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of a positive entity is admitted to be removable by knowledge, the direct perception of ignorance—which inherently contains the cognition of its locus and object in the form "I am ignorant"—is indeed contradicted. Reply: Not so. All three—the cognitions of the locus, the object, and [the ignorance itself]—are manifested by the single witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Thus, while this witness establishes both the locus and the object, it likewise establishes the ignorance itself; it does not remove it. It is only the knowledge consisting of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti-jñāna*) that removes it. And since that [removing knowledge] is not present here, how can there be any contradiction?

If it is argued that in the cognition "I do not know the jar," the jar—which serves to distinguish the ignorance—is not capable of being perceived by the Witness (sākṣin) when devoid of a connection [to it]; for the establishment of external objects depends upon a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) connected to the self, and furthermore, ignorance is something to be removed by a means of knowledge—then this is true. However, although the jar in its bare form is not an object of the Witness, its perception is indeed possible through the Witness when it possesses a connection [to the jar] by way of ignorance, as qualified by the attribute of being unknown (ajñātatva).

Nor should it be argued that if the pure [object] lacks being known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedyatva*), then its being so known as a qualified entity is also untenable, because we do not observe that taste and the like—which are qualified by visual substances—are themselves visual objects; for even though the isolated atom lacks mental perceptibility (*mānasapratyakṣatva*), others accept that it is an object of mental perception as a qualifier in the cognition "I know the atom. Furthermore, in common experience, although Rāhu is not perceived in isolation, he is observed to be perceived when eclipsed by the moon or other such bodies.

Even in the opponent’s view, in the case of the cognition "I do not know the jar," a refutation has already been stated regarding whether the jar—the qualifier of the absence of knowledge—is perceived or not perceived. Therefore, every object is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), whether in its state of being known or in its state of being unknown. If it is objected: "In that case, there would be no distinction between objects that are known and those that are unknown; furthermore, the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would be rendered useless, and there would be a contradiction with the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) [of the means of cognition]," we reply: "Not so."

Just as ignorance, having produced the property of "unknowability" (ajñātatva) in its own object, brings about its connection with the Witness (sākṣin), so too, by accepting that valid cognition (pramāṇa) also brings about the property of "knowability" (jñātatva) in its own object and thereby effects its connection with the Witness, the aforementioned defect is avoided. Thus, the perception "I am ignorant," supported by the arguments stated above, is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) for ignorance in the form of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa).

Nevertheless, for those who take pleasure solely in inference, this is also stated—just like perception—to establish its positive nature directly, without depending on further logical justification: "The subject under dispute, which is valid knowledge, must be preceded by another entity located in the same space as itself, which is distinct from its own prior non-existence, which veils its own object, and which is removed by it; because it illuminates an object not previously illuminated, like the light of a lamp first produced in the dark."

If "mere cognition" were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the case of a cognition that is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); this has been stated [previously] as "it is a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, the term "disputed" (*vimata*) is used to exclude the continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika*). If it were simply said "preceded by a real entity" (*vastupūrvaka*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) with respect to its own substratum, such as the Self (*ātman*); therefore, the term "another real entity" (*vastvantara*) is employed.

Likewise, by means of the four qualifiers beginning with "in its own location" (*svadeśa*), it excludes—in descending order—the causal complex distinct from its own substrate (*svāśraya*), such as merit (*dharma*) and the like, prior cognition, and antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). By this much, the intended specific object, which is ignorance in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa-ajñāna*), is established. The term "unmanifested" (*aprakāśita*) is used to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*). The term "first" (*prathama*) is used to exclude the deficiency of light in a continuous stream of illumination. The term "in darkness" (*andhakāre*) is used to exclude the case of the light of a lamp produced in a place already possessed of sunlight.

The indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the material cause of the twofold superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—consisting of both knowledge and objects—is established by the fact that such superimposition would otherwise be inexplicable. Nor is it possible for it to be explained otherwise; for if it were real, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that its effects would also be real. Furthermore, its beginninglessness (*anāditva*) follows from the fact that it cannot otherwise serve as the root cause. If it were beginningless, then, given the requirement of a succession of material causes, a root cause could not be established.

Thus, it is established that beginningless, indeterminable, positive ignorance (ajñāna), which resides in the Self and has the Self as its object, is the material cause (upādāna) of superimposition (adhyāsa). Therefore, it is proven that beginningless, indeterminable, positive ignorance, residing in the Self and having the Self as its object, is the material cause of superimposition.

Now, one might ask: does this ignorance veil the non-self just as it veils the self, or does it not? Not the first alternative, because there would be neither a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor a purpose for such a claim. To explain: it would have to be apprehended by a means of knowledge that "this blue object is veiled by ignorance," yet that is impossible both when the blue is perceived and when it is not. If you think that even though the veiling by ignorance is impossible at the very time the blue is cognized, the veiling existing at a time prior to the cognition of the blue is nonetheless understood, that is not so; for no means of establishing such a cognition can be specified.

Is it the fact of being cognized at this moment that serves as the indicator? Or is it the restriction "only now"? Or is it the inexplicability otherwise of the recognition "this is that very same blue"? Or rather, is it the inexplicability otherwise of the absence of both cognition and memory between the two acts of perception and recognition? Not the first; for in the case of continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), since that which was cognized previously is cognized again later, the fact of being cognized "now" is possible even without a prior veil [of ignorance].

Not the second, because of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*): the establishment of the restriction "only now" depends on the establishment of the prior and subsequent concealments, and the establishment of the latter depends on the establishment of the former. Not the third, because there is no rule that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) occurs only for something previously known that has been forgotten for some time; for we observe the recognition "That is I" even when the self is manifest at all times.

Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because it could equally well be argued that even among those cognitions that have arisen between two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and a subsequent recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is an absence of memory precisely because they are free from obscuration (*āvaraṇa*). Indeed, there is no rule that whatever has been experienced must necessarily be remembered. Nor should it be said: "I do not know the object you mentioned," for the cognition of the relation with the object is experienced, and since that relation is observed in the self as the very nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*) which acts as an obscuration, how can it be denied?

This is because it is accepted that the witnessing consciousness experiences the ignorance, its object, and their relationship—all of which are superimposed upon itself. Furthermore, the relationship between ignorance and its object is characterized by the relation of cause and effect, not by the relation of the veiler and the veiled; for that which is superimposed cannot be subject to concealment. At the time of its manifestation, concealment is contradicted; at the time of non-manifestation, however, it does not exist at all, since that which is superimposed has a body consisting solely of its appearance, like a double moon.

If that which is superimposed were also concealed, then its manifestation would never occur at any time; for since the superimposed object is not within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no removal of its concealment. Indeed, an object accessible through valid cognition, because it possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*), may persist even when unperceived and thus might somehow be concealed; but how could that which is superimposed—which is to be removed by valid cognition—possibly be concealed? Therefore, there is simply no evidence for the concealment of the non-self (*anātman*).

Likewise, the purpose [of the veil] is difficult to establish; for in every case, the purpose of a veil is the obstruction of a light that is already present. Therefore, in this context, is the self-luminosity of the non-self something that is already established, or is it established by the force of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or by the force of consciousness (*caitanya*)? It cannot be the first, because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*). Nor can it be the second, because a veil that is to be removed by a means of knowledge cannot logically act as an obstruction to that very means. Nor can it be the third, because if that [self-luminosity] is already established simply through the existence of a veil over consciousness, it is redundant to postulate a separate veil for the non-self.

For when the sun is obstructed by Mount Meru, an umbrella or the like is not required to block its heat and light. Now, if it were argued that—just as even when the sun is covered by clouds one requires an umbrella and so forth to block the subtle heat known as "warmth"—so too here, a separate veil is required to ward off even the slightest trace of illumination produced by consciousness when it is veiled by ignorance; that is incorrect.

Is it accepted that there is only one ignorance which has the Self as its locus and veils the non-Self, or is a distinct ignorance postulated for each object? Not the first, because the manifestation of an object is impossible without the destruction of its veil; furthermore, if ignorance were removed by the knowledge of a single thing, it would follow that liberation occurs immediately. Nor the second, because there is no basis for such a postulation; rather, we accept that there is a mere glimmer of light produced by consciousness when it is veiled by ignorance. Otherwise, the conventional usage "this is unknown" could not be established.

Therefore, because it is devoid of both proof and purpose, the position that there is an obscuration is difficult to maintain. Nor is the second [position] tenable, because if there were no obscuration, it would follow that the non-self would be perceived at all times.

To this it is replied: The first [alternative] is simply not accepted. As for the second, how can there be cognition at all times? Is it by way of being known (*jñātatā*), or by way of being unknown (*ajñātatā*), or perhaps sometimes by way of being known and at other times by way of being unknown? Not the first, because the operation of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that produces "being known" is only occasional. Not the second, because "being unknown" ceases after some time due to "being known. Not the third, because it is accepted [by us]. For it has been said: "Every object is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*), either by way of being known or by way of being unknown."

Surely, "unknowability" (ajñātatva) means being the object of ignorance (ajñāna). And being an object means being the locus of a specific excellence produced by the subject. Now, since it is not admitted that an obscuration caused by ignorance exists in what is not the Self (anātman), how can that [non-Self] possess unknowability? It is said in reply: Ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the "this-ness" of the mother-of-pearl shell produces the superimposition of silver and thereby effects an excellence called its manifestation upon the shell; thus, the unknowability of the shell is established.
