Thus, in all cases, even though no obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is admitted in that which is non-self (*anātman*), it should be understood as something to be known (*veditavya*). Now, one might object: "In the case of the projection (*vikṣepa*) called silver, it does not appear while the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is being known, because that [silver] is to be removed by the knowledge of the mother-of-pearl. But if the mother-of-pearl is unknown, how can that excess—the projection—be apprehended? This is not so; for there is no removal of the two defects [of error], namely: "the form of the mother-of-pearl is not known" and "the form of 'this' (*idam*) is known."

Now, even on this view that ignorance is one and has the self as its locus, and that it produces only *vikṣepa* (projection) and not *āvaraṇa* (concealment), must the projection alone be dissolved into its material cause by the knowledge of the shell—as a jar is destroyed by a mace—or is the material cause itself also removed? In the first case, if by the knowledge of Brahman only the projection were dissolved in that same manner, the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣāpatti*). In the second case, since ignorance would be removed by the knowledge of the shell alone, there would be the undesirable contingency of immediate liberation (*sadyomukti-prasaṅga*).

If it is maintained that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) has ignorance (*ajñāna*) as its material cause (*upādāna*), then, out of a desire to avoid the consequence of immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*) upon the dawn of knowledge, or else if one accepts that there is a distinct ignorance for each object, two faults would follow: the charge of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) and the falsity of superimposition. This is not so; first of all, there is no fault in the former position. For the following inference holds: "The subject under discussion, which is knowledge of Brahman, removes the material cause of the projection (*vikṣepa*), because, while being opposed to it, it occurs subsequently [to the projection]; just as the knowledge of mother-of-pearl removes both its own prior absence and the superimposition of silver. Thus, by means of this inference, there is no error.

Even in the second alternative, the aforementioned defect does not exist, because it is accepted that the specific states (*avasthābheda*) of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) themselves—which serve as the material causes (*upādāna*) for silver and so forth—are what are removed by the cognitions of the mother-of-pearl and other such objects. Thus, there is no defect whatsoever in not accepting an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) in the case of insentient things (*jaḍa*). As for the statement "obscuring its own object" (*svaviṣayāvaraṇa*) used in the inference proving positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*), that applies exactly as it stands to the case of the Self (*ātman*).

However, regarding insentient objects like the mother-of-pearl, the specific states of ignorance which are the material causes of silver and so forth function as an obscuration only by virtue of their result—namely, by acting as a mediator (*vyavadhāyaka*) between consciousness and the object—and not directly; thus, there is no contradiction.

Now, regarding the self as well, what is this so-called "obscuration"? Is it the destruction of light, or an impediment to the production of the effect known as the manifestation of the object, or perhaps the waiting for another auxiliary factor in that very process? It cannot be the first, because light is of the nature of the eternal consciousness of the self. Nor can it be the second or third, because we do not admit a separate manifestation in the object apart from the light of consciousness manifested through a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*). Therefore, if you argue that the nature of obscuration is difficult to define, that is true.

For this very reason, one must accept that the veil (*āvaraṇa*) consists of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*); its denial on the mere ground of its being difficult to define is not tenable, because it is established by inference. To explain: there certainly exists among the ignorant a common usage such as, "The reality of the Self, which transcends hunger and so forth and is well-known to the wise, neither exists nor shines forth."

This empirical usage regarding the Self must be caused by an obscuration in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa-āvaraṇa*), because, while the full causes for such usages as "it exists" and "it manifests" are present, there occurs a usage contrary to them; for that which is not thus [caused] is not so [contrary], just like the usage "the pot exists and manifests. Nor is the completeness of the causes unestablished, because there is no dependence on anything else here beyond the eternally established self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-caitanya*). Nor is there an alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*).

Because it is difficult to establish a covering for a corporeal substance that is distinct from this [self] within a self that is partless and all-pervading; thus, it is established that the nature of the covering consists in its fitness for the aforementioned empirical usage regarding the self.

If it is argued: "In the term *ajñāna* (ignorance), if the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-existence (*abhāva*), then it would mean the 'non-existence of knowledge'; if its meaning is opposition (*virodha*), it would mean 'erroneous knowledge' (*bhrāntijñāna*); and if its meaning is something else, it would mean 'the latent impression of error' (*bhrāntisaṃskāra*). Thus, it is simply the non-existence of knowledge, erroneous knowledge, and its impressions that are designated as 'ignorance,' and these alone, by obstructing the manifestation of the reality of Brahman, will produce the aforementioned worldly transactions—what is the use of postulating this positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) called 'veiling' (*āvaraṇa')? This is not so.

This is because the non-appearance of the reality of Brahman during deep sleep and similar states cannot be accounted for otherwise. To explain: is the non-appearance of the reality of Brahman there due to its own nature, or is it because, as with the cognition of another person, the reality of Brahman appears as distinct from the witnessing individual soul (*jīva*), or is it due to some obstruction? It cannot be the first, because Brahman is self-luminous. Nor can it be the second, because of the scriptural text "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which teaches their identity.

Regarding the third [alternative], is the obstruction due to erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), or rather due to its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), or perhaps due to the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*), or else due to the power of karma (*karmavaśāt*)? It cannot be the first, because even false cognition has ceased during deep sleep and similar states. It cannot be the second, because the latent impression of the error of silver is not observed to obstruct the manifestation of the true nature of the mother-of-pearl. As for the third, the absence of the eternal self-nature cognition (*svarūpajñāna*) is simply not possible.

However, the absence of other cognitions is not capable of obstructing the manifestation of the self-luminous reality of Brahman; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such obstruction persisting even in liberation. Regarding the fourth alternative as well, do the karmas obstruct the entirety of consciousness, or do they do so while excluding its own manifesting aspect? In the first case, since there would be no means of proof, the karmas themselves could never be established. Nor is the second case tenable, as it would lead to the fallacy of the "half-old woman" argument (applying a partial standard without scriptural authority).

Nor should it be argued that the defects of conceptualization (vikalpa) are equally applicable even when the obscuration is positive in nature; for the abandonment of the self-luminous aspect—though it may appear as a "half-old-woman" (ardhajaratīya) compromise—is postulated because otherwise the immediate experience of the ignorant person would be inexplicable. However, actions are not experienced as immediate in that way. Even if, in that case, indirect experience (parokṣānubhava) itself were the postulator [of the obscuration], nevertheless, actions are not obstructive factors because they exist in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra), like the impression of the error of silver.

If it be objected that, according to the Smṛti passage, "Knowledge veils darkness and produces heedlessness," it is the quality of *tamas* alone that must be the obstacle, we say: no. For if that [quality] were not removed by the knowledge of Brahman, there would follow the consequence of the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*). If, however, it is removed, then since it itself is a positive obscuration (*bhāvarūpāvaraṇa*), the dispute would be merely over a name.

Therefore, even the proponent of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābhedavādin*) must abandon this stubborn insistence that the absence of knowledge alone is the cause for the non-manifestation of the reality of Brahman during deep sleep, and must instead accept ignorance as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpājñāna*).

As for that other stubborn insistence of his—that the delusion "I am a human being" during waking and dreaming states is itself the cause for the non-manifestation of the reality of Brahman—that too is incorrect; for in his own system, it is difficult to maintain that such a delusion exists.

Just as in the case of the expressions "the brindled cow" and "the hornless cow," where—by virtue of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of both terms with respect to the single universal *gotva* (cowness)—both difference and non-difference between that universal and each of the two individuals are accepted as being established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), why is it not likewise accepted that for a single individual soul (*jīva*), both difference and non-difference from both the body and Brahman are established by valid means of knowledge, such as in the cognitions "I am a man" and "I am Brahman"? And thus, the cognition of non-difference between the body and the self in the form "I am a man" would also be established by valid means of knowledge, and not an error (*bhrānti*).

The scriptural negation, "I am not a human being, but Brahman," is likewise valid, just as the statement, "This is not a spotted cow, but a hornless one. Now, if it be argued that—just as there is a negation, "This is not silver," with respect to the perceived substrate of "this-ness"—so too, since there is a negation of humanity, "I am not a human being," with respect to the perceived substrate of the Self, the perception of humanity in the Self must be an error—that is not so.

If that were the case, then when a cow is apprehended in the form of "Khaṇḍa" (the broken-horned one) with the universal "cowness" as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the subsequent negation "This is not Khaṇḍa" would entail that even the cognition of Khaṇḍa is an error. Nor can it be argued that it is Khaṇḍa who is negated, rather than [his identity] within the limiting adjunct of cowness; for Khaṇḍa is not even applicable to a *muṇḍa* (a hornless cow).

If it is argued that "cowness" as delimited by an individual such as Khaṇḍa is the recognized substrate (upādhi), and that it is not "cowness" delimited by Khaṇḍa that is negated there, but rather "cowness" as delimited by an individual such as Muṇḍa—then in the present case as well, the Self as delimited by "humanity" is the recognized substrate; and it is not "humanity" that is negated there, but rather [the Self] as delimited by "Brahman-hood."

If this were so, then just as the individual bodies *khaṇḍa* and *muṇḍa* are connected by a genus (*gotva*) that persists through them, the body and Brahman would be connected by a persisting Self (*ātman*). Consequently, the validity of the cognition "I am a human being"—just like the cognition "this is a *khaṇḍa* cow"—would be unavoidable. Now, if you argue that its validity here is due to the non-interruption of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), then that is equally the case in the present instance as well; for even in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), according to your view, the individual soul (*jīva*), being non-different from Brahman—the omniscient cause of all—possesses the nature of the Universal Self, and thus the transaction consisting of the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding all bodies, senses, and so forth, is not interrupted.

First of all, it is untenable that these five factors—genus, individual, cause, effect, quality, qualified, qualifier, qualified, part, and whole—which serve as the grounds for establishing difference and non-difference, act as such grounds collectively, because this is contradicted by observed instances of deviation. However, if each one acts as a ground individually, then since you yourself have admitted the cumbersome complexity of having multiple grounds, why should the relationship between the body and the embodied soul not also be a ground?

If this [reason] is not effective, then it could be applied in the same way to other cases as well; thus, neither difference nor non-difference would ever be established. If, out of fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), you insist that [the relation] applies only to these five, then let there be a cause-and-effect relationship between the body and the self, since it is possible to metaphorically attribute to the self the causality residing in Brahman by virtue of their commonality in being conscious (*cetanatva*).

If it is argued that only a primary relationship (*mukhya-sambandha*) is the cause [of valid cognition], and therefore, due to the absence of such a relationship, the cognition "I am a human" is an error (*bhrānti*), even so, if this so-called error is a modification (*pariṇāma*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then ignorance (*avidyā*) would not have the Self as its locus. If it is argued that the modification of the internal organ itself is superimposed upon the Self, even then, according to your view—which maintains the theory of misapprehension of another object (*anyathākhyāti*)—the connection between the Self and ignorance would not exist, because the relation between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed object (*āropya*) is non-existent. If, on the other hand, it is argued that error is a modification of the Self, we say no.

Because the self is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). If it is argued that the unchanging nature of the self is unproven for us, that is true; nevertheless, you accept that the self possesses the attribute of eternal knowledge (*nityajñāna*), and thus while that knowledge remains, a transformation into the form of error must be asserted. But that is not logical, because two specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the same kind cannot simultaneously inhere in a single substance when neither has reached a state of destruction. Indeed, two instances of whiteness are never seen to inhere simultaneously in a single cloth.
Therefore, even in the states of waking and dreaming, one must admit that the veiling of Brahman is indeed beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*ajñāna*).

If it is objected that if there were a connection with ignorance, the soul’s quality of being unattached (*asaṅgatva*) would be destroyed, we say no; for the connection itself, like ignorance, is beginningless and imagined, and thus—just like its own effects—it does not destroy the soul’s unattached nature.

Thus, positive ignorance, without veiling the non-self, produces therein mere mental agitation (*vikṣepa*); but by veiling the self, it further produces superimpositions (*adhyāsa*) suitable for worldly transaction, such as "I am this" and "this is mine."

Surely, the partless conscious self (cidātman) is perceived as "I," and not in a form permeated by two parts as in the case of "this is silver"; therefore, this is not a superimposition (adhyāsa). Likewise, the body is also perceived as "this. Furthermore, its status as a superimposed object is impossible, because it is apprehended by the sense organs which constitute valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). If it were a superimposed object, it would have to be cognizable solely through the witness-consciousness (sākṣi-pratyakṣa), like ignorance (ajñāna).

Although the relationship between the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed object (*āropya*) appears to exist here as having two parts—just as in the cognition "this is silver," where one perceives "I am a human"—nevertheless, this is not an invariable rule. For when the self departs [from the body], the body is perceived separately; indeed, a superimposed silver is never perceived apart from its substratum.

Now, if you should think that the means of knowledge which perceives the body is merely empirical and does not reveal ultimate reality, even so, if [the body] were superimposed upon the Self, its dissolution would have to occur in that very [Self]. But it is not heard [in scripture] to be so; rather, the dissolution is heard to occur in earth alone, as in "the body [dissolves] into earth. Therefore, this [body] is not superimposed upon the Self.

Likewise, the notion "this is mine" (mamedam) also perceives a collection of objects related to the agent of the "I-notion" (ahaṃkartṛ), which are distinct from the body and unfit to be the object of the "I-notion"; yet, there is not even a suspicion of superimposition (adhyāsa) regarding them. To this it is replied: first, we shall demonstrate that the inert (jaḍa) portion is included within the "I-notion," and therefore that [notion] is indeed a case of superimposition. Furthermore, since the body—like the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and the senses—is an object of perception (dṛśyatva), its status as superimposed must be established.

And because the internal organ and the senses are never perceived as having existence apart from the Self, their status as superimposed is established through the immediacy of the pure witness-consciousness (sākṣin), just like ignorance (ajñāna).

Nor should it be suspected that superimposition occurs for them only through association and not in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*); for in the very passage, "His vital breaths do not depart," it is stated that "they are completely dissolved" (*samavalīyante*) when there is the realization of the reality of the Self, and thus dissolution into the Self is taught. From this, superimposition is established even in terms of essential nature. It should be understood that the body also dissolves into the Self alone by way of the earth. When the enjoyer, characterized by the body, senses, and so forth, is superimposed, then what need is there to say that the external objects of enjoyment, which serve as his instruments, are likewise superimposed?

For the royal paraphernalia of a king created in a dream or by a magician's trickery does not possess ultimate reality. Therefore, these three—“I,” “this,” and “mine”—are all merely superimpositions (*adhyāsa*). Nor should one dispute that there is superimposition even of a mere attribute, since we observe the superimposition of the attribute of deafness alone upon the self in the expression, "I am deaf. As for the superimposition of cognition, it need not be established separately because it is inseparable from the superimposition of objects. Thus, it is established that this superimposition, being grounded in experience, cannot be denied.
Whether they be teacher and disciple or two disputants investigating reality according to the scripture, the teacher first explained superimposition (adhyāsa) to the disciple. ||1||

Now, with reference to those who dispute this superimposition (adhyāsa), its definition, as well as the grounds for its possibility and its means of valid cognition, are stated for the purpose of establishing superimposition. || 2 ||

Now, it may be objected that everywhere a definiendum is distinguished from others by means of its definition, while the notion of its impossibility regarding its own place, time, and conditions is dispelled through probability, and its actual existence is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, in this case as well, the means of knowledge—namely perception, inference, the inexplicability of worldly practice (*vyavahārānyathānupapatti*), and scripture—which will be presented for the proof of superimposition, effectively result in the exclusion of superimposition from other things and the removal of the notion of its impossibility, even if not explicitly stated.

If it is argued that since superimposition (*adhyāsa*) which is both non-excluded and impossible cannot be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the definition and its possibility need not be described separately from the means of knowledge—this is not so. For here, the form of superimposition is twofold: the nature of one thing as another, and falsity (*mithyātva*). Among these, falsity cannot be experienced through perception and other means that are being presented as the proof for "one thing being the nature of another," because falsity is understood only through the impossibility of sublation (*bādhānupapatti*) in cases such as "this is silver."

And here, too, there is an absence of sublation (*bādhā*). If it is argued that even here there is indeed sublation—because, in the absence of a mutual distinction (*itaretaraviveka*), it is impossible to understand that this appearance of one thing as having the nature of another is caused by sublation—we say: not so. For even though there may be a logical sublation (*yauktikabādha*), since there is no immediate sublation (*aparokṣabādha*) that cuts away the manifestation of the illusion, the determination of its falsity remains indistinct. Therefore, in order to make that [falsity] distinct, the definition itself must be stated.

Similarly, even when something like a solar eclipse—an adventitious phenomenon—is understood through worldly knowledge that is free from causes for invalidity, a sense of improbability arises due to its non-perception [in the past]. Likewise, in this case of the Self as well, because one perceives attributes such as being non-objective (*aviṣayatva*), incorporeality (*asaṅgatva*), and the absence of similarity (*sādṛśyābhāva*)—which are properties opposed to superimposition—a cognition of improbability arises. Nor should it be argued: "If the Self in its form as non-objective and so forth is not known, there can be no cognition of improbability; but if it is known, then superimposition cannot exist at all."

Because the appearance of something as remote is a cause for the thought that it is impossible, and because the superimposition of immediacy is not removed by that alone; therefore, in order to dispel the notion of impossibility, probability (saṃbhāvanā) must indeed be stated separately from the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).

Accordingly, others also have stated that the means of valid knowledge is preceded by the definition (lakṣaṇa) and probability: "The establishment of the object of knowledge depends on the means of knowledge, and the establishment of the means of knowledge depends on its definition."
And that [invalidity] cannot be prevented even by the gods, when it occurs within the means of valid cognition such as direct perception.
A position that has been formally proposed in a thesis may be established by means of a reason;
however, there is no protection for it against reasons if it is destroyed at the very moment of its arising.

Even there, the possibility [of superimposition] is preceded by its definition. For only when the distinct nature [of the objects] has been established by means of a definition does it become appropriate to subsequently investigate whether such a thing is possible or not; otherwise, the investigation would be without a subject matter. Therefore, the definition must be stated first. That is stated as follows: Superimposition is indeed twofold—either an object qualified by cognition, or a cognition qualified by an object.

In this regard, first concerning the object (*artha*), the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is: another object, which is similar to that which is being remembered, appearing under the nature of something else. Regarding cognition (*jñāna*), however, the definition is: the appearance of one thing as having the nature of another, which is similar to memory.

If it is argued—as the proponents of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*) maintain—that in the case of "this is silver," since there is an absence of means of valid cognition such as the eye, it follows by elimination that it is only the remembered silver that appears, and not something similar to it—this is not so; for [the object] appears as being situated in front [of the observer]. Nor should it be thought that it is only the "this" portion (*idamaṃśa*) that appears in that way, and not the "silver" portion.

Just as in cases such as "this is a silver pot" regarding a correctly perceived locus, the universal and the particular appear as immediate cognitions in a state of mutual conjunction, so too do they appear here [in the case of the shell-silver]. Now, if it is argued that such conventional usage arises from the appearance of the universal and the particular in uninterrupted proximity, and not from the actual existence of a cognition of their conjunction—that is not so; for even in the case of a real object, no deficiency whatsoever is observed. If it is argued that the deficiency consists precisely in the absence of silver in front of one, we say no; for...

Is the determination of the absence of silver due to the absence of immediate consciousness, or is it due to the sublating cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) "this is not silver"? It cannot be the first, because the very absence of consciousness is not admitted. If the absence of consciousness were determined solely by the absence of the object, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*). Therefore, precisely because of the existence of immediate consciousness, the existence of the silver present before one must be accepted.

Nor should it be said that the determination of the existence of consciousness depends on the determination of the existence of the object through a reversal [of the process]; for if that were so, the determination of the object would likewise depend on another determination, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress. Therefore, the determination of consciousness is self-evident, and the existence of the object depends upon it. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because a subsequent cognition that contradicts a prior cognition—such as "this is silver"—would lack the power to sublate it.

If it is asked, "What then is the status of the subsequent cognition? [we reply: it will be exactly the same as the status of the prior cognition according to your own view. Just as you have postulated a non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between the form of "this" and the form of "silver" in the case of "This is silver," why not likewise postulate that even in the case of negation, there is merely non-discrimination and not a cognition of a relation (*saṃsarga-saṃvit*)? If it is argued that the existence of a cognition of the relation of negation is determined by the knowledge of the correspondence with practical activity (*vyavahāra-saṃvāda*), then the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition would be lost.

If it is argued that there is no departure from one’s own tenets (apasiddhānta) because this proof is directed only at one who holds a contrary view, even so, the infinite regress (anavasthā) remains difficult to avoid. Nor should it be said that the absence of silver in front of one is universally accepted; for we admit that the illusory silver, which is capable of being sublated by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, exists precisely as it appears. If it is further argued that even with the admission of illusory silver, this contradicts the threefold negation "this is not silver," we say: no.

This is because that negation has as its object both the silver well-known in the world and the silver of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor should it be suspected that this is a negation of what is not even applicable (*aprasakta-pratiṣedha*); for, since one observes the engagement of a person seeking real silver toward silver that is illusory, the applicability of "being real silver" must be admitted within the general category (*sāmānyopādhi*). Otherwise, even the negation of a jar on the ground would be difficult to maintain: if the jar were present, the negation would be contradicted; if the jar were absent, there would be no negation of what is not applicable.

Therefore, the application of the term "jar" occurs through the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of common place and common time, but not directly. Let it be the same for the ultimately real silver (*paramārtha-rajata*). This being so, both the subsequent cognition "there is no silver here," which has the ultimately real silver as its object, and the cognition "silver appeared falsely," which has the illusory silver (*mithyā-rajata*) as its object, are justified. Otherwise, one of the two cognitions would have to be denied.

If it is argued that the conceptualization of false silver—the labor of which is undertaken by postulating a "manifestation of a complex" (saṃsṛṣṭāvabhāsa) due to the impossibility of the immediate presentation of silver—is done for the sake of making that [immediacy] possible; whereas the immediacy of silver is actually possible even without a manifestation of a complex, simply through the non-discrimination (aviveka) from the immediate cognition of the mother-of-pearl—[we reply: No, for if that were so, at the time of the discriminative cognition, one would have to reflect upon the very non-discrimination itself, thinking, "Until this moment, that silver was not discriminated from this [mother-of-pearl]," yet it is not reflected upon in such a manner.

However, by the recognition "this appeared as silver for so long," it is precisely a mixed appearance that is being recalled. Therefore, one must admit the existence of false silver present before one; otherwise, how could the statement "having seen the mother-of-pearl, he acts toward silver" be consistent?

Consequently, this silver is not something being remembered, but rather something resembling what was remembered. And that similarity is established because it is apprehended by a cognition dependent upon a prior experience; indeed, no delusion of silver is observed in one who has never experienced silver.

For this very reason, since it is produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it should be understood that the superimposition of cognition (*jñānādhyāsa*) shares the same nature as memory. If it is argued: "The subject under dispute [the superimposition] is not born of a latent impression, because it is a cognition distinct from memory, like perception"—this is not so; for being produced by mere sensory contact (*saṃprayoga*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor should one suspect that the probandum (*sādhya*) does not pervade [the reason] in the case of cognitions derived from inference, scripture, and so forth; for since these depend upon the cognition of the pervader (*vyāpya*) and other factors, they are themselves born of latent impressions, and thus the absence of the probandum exists within them.

It might be argued as follows: "The cognition under dispute is in accordance with reality, because it is a cognition, like a [previously] accepted one. By this logic, knowledge consists of only two categories: valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and memory (*smṛti*). Consequently, even the cognition of silver is not an illusory superimposition (*adhyāsa*), but rather memory, because it is produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), just like the accepted case. Nor should it be asked why, given its status as memory, another piece of mother-of-pearl is not remembered due to extreme similarity; for the defects residing in the agent, such as passion (*rāga*), also serve as causes, and these are absent in the case of another piece of mother-of-pearl.

Due to those very defects, the memory of silver has its aspect of "that-ness" (tattā) obscured; thus, in the recollection of silver, that specific element is not manifested. Likewise, because the capacity to manifest the particularities is obstructed by those same defects, even in the perception of the mother-of-pearl, qualities such as its bluish back are not manifested. Consequently, both the perception and the recollection become indistinct from one another, and therefore the person seeking silver proceeds toward the object present before them.

Now, are both perception and memory motivators for action, or is it each one individually? If the former, do they act together or successively? Not the first, because there is no simultaneity between perception and memory. It is untenable that the two, distinguished by their sequence, are motivators; for a preceding cognition, being separated [in time] from the activity, cannot be its cause. Nor can each one individually be a motivator, because practical activity has a specific object as its domain.

If it is argued that the cognition of a relation (*saṃsṛṣṭapratyaya*) is desired for the sake of initiating a specific activity, we say no; for it is the uninterrupted arising of perception and memory that functions as the motivator. If it is argued that the cognition of a relation is recognized in the form "this appeared as silver," we say no; because that is merely a conventional expression (*vyavahāra*).

As for the appearance of bitterness in what is actually sweet that occurs in a newborn infant—inferable from such acts as spitting—that too is simply the recollection of bitterness experienced in a previous birth, and not a relational cognition (saṃsarga-pratyaya) consisting of error. However, due to the defect of bile (pitta), the specific quality of sweetness and the element of "that-ness" (tattā) are not manifested in the acts of perception and recollection. Furthermore, the statement by the author of the Bhāṣya, "And what was experienced in another birth is not remembered," refers to the general rule (prāyika).

Otherwise, there would be no inclination toward activities such as suckling at the breast, because the memory of it being a means to a desired end would be absent. Even on the view that it is an error (*bhrānti*), experience in a previous birth must be accepted as the cause; otherwise, since all [past] experiences are indistinguishable in their nature as having been experienced, even the "seventh flavor" (*saptama-rasa*) might appear in such an error. If it is argued that the author of the treatise himself has shown that the superimposition (*saṃsarga-āropa*) is an error by stating "the cognition of reality in what is not real," we say no; for that statement was intended with reference to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

If it is asked, "Since the causality of a cognition of relation (*saṃsargajñāna*) is pervaded by [occurrence in] correct instances, why is it abandoned here?", we reply: "Because of complexity (*gaurava*). Even for one who maintains the theory of error (*bhrāntivādin*), a non-discrimination between perception and memory must necessarily be accepted as the cause of that [error]. And since the activity is established by that alone—which is admitted by both parties—what is the use of an additional cognition of relation? Therefore, the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) alone is logical.

To this it is replied: What is this so-called "non-apprehension" (*akhyāti*)? Is it merely the absence of apprehension; or is it a cognition that causes one who desires one thing to engage with something else; or is it the cognition of multiple undifferentiated objects? In the first case, there would be delusion (*bhrama*) even in deep sleep, and not during waking or dreaming. In the second case, there would be no delusion in instances where no action occurs due to sudden sublation or laziness.

Regarding the third [alternative] as well: what is this so-called "distinctness from the counter-correlative of non-distinctness"? Is it the apprehension of difference? Or the non-apprehension of non-difference? Or perhaps a cognition qualified by mutual absence, difference, duality, and so forth? It cannot be the first, because once the difference between the universal and the particular has been apprehended—by virtue of being the cause for the recollection of two non-synonymous words, namely "this" and "silver"—non-distinction is impossible.

The second [alternative] is not tenable; for, since difference has already been apprehended in the manner described, when its opposite—non-difference—is apprehended, it is impossible to establish the non-distinction [of the two] by negating that [prior] apprehension of difference. As for the third [alternative], is it required that the cognition of duality and so forth be direct (*āhatya*)? Or is even an incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) cognition sufficient? In the first case, in the sentence "Bring the cow with a stick," non-distinction would result, because duality and so forth are not directly perceived in relation to both the cow and the stick.
In the second case, there would be no non-distinction between the object in front and the silver, since an incidental cognition of duality and so forth exists between them as well.

If it is argued: "Surely, even if non-discrimination cannot be established by depending on the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), let it be established by way of the substratum (*dharmin*)," that too is incorrect. First of all, non-discrimination between two substrata that are being perceived is impossible, because they appear clearly as non-identical. If you mean non-discrimination between those not being perceived, then an error would follow even during deep sleep.

If it is argued that non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is indeed the non-apprehension of non-relation (*asaṃsargāgraha*), and that this is possible in the case of the perceived "this" and "silver" because one never observes the cognition "this and silver are unrelated," then even so, what is intended by "non-apprehension of non-relation"? Is it the non-apprehension of non-relation between the perception and the memory themselves? Or between any two things whatsoever? Or between those two cognitions that are devoid of a cognition of relation? In the first case, the illusion "I am a human being" would not occur; for both [the self and the humanity] would be objects of perception.

In the second case, even such [cognitions] as "the cow is broken" or "the cloth is white" would be erroneous, because there is no cognition of a relation [between the two terms]. In the third case as well, that same defect remains; for a cognition of relation is not possible, since the unity that constitutes its object is absent. And that unity is understood to be the object of that [cognition] in the case of recognition (pratyabhijñā).

If it is argued that the object of that [cognition] is merely the relation between quality and qualified and so forth, and not identity, then in the case of "this is silver" as well, since it could be said that the object is the relation of similarity, the cognition of a relation (saṃsarga-pratyaya) would be unavoidable. Now, if it is argued that in that case, because of the sublation by the cognition of non-relation—namely, "this is not silver"—neither the relation nor its cognition can possibly exist;

In that case, according to your own view, even in instances such as quality and the possessor of quality, there certainly exists a non-relation cognition known as the cognition of mutual absence; thus, since relation and its cognition would be impossible, the consequence of error remains unavoidable. Therefore, non-apprehension of non-relation is also not what constitutes non-discrimination (aviveka).

Now, one might object: "By one who censures non-discrimination (aviveka), some means of discrimination (vivecaka) must be specified here. First of all, perception does not distinguish its own object from that which is being remembered, because its capacity to manifest specific features is obstructed by defects. Nor is remembrance capable of distinguishing its own object from that which is being perceived, because the conviction of remembrance has been stolen away. If this is argued, it is not so; for the capacity to distinguish is easily established for both.

For instance: do you maintain that this difference pertains only to the forms of "this" (*idam*) and "silver" (*rajata*) as qualified by their respective universals (*jāti*) and individuals (*vyakti*), or even to them in their mere form alone? It cannot be the first, because since there is no difference—and thus identity—between the forms of "this" and "silver" under discussion when they are unqualified by universals and so forth, it would follow that there is a cognition of the relation between those two objects.

Regarding the second [position] as well: does the first cognition grasp the object, and the second cognition apprehend the relationship between the substratum (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), after which the difference (*bheda*) is grasped by a third cognition; or is the difference grasped simultaneously with the object itself? In the first case, since all cognitions of objects would precede the grasping of difference, it follows that they would be erroneous due to having undifferentiated objects.

In the second case, since the difference is already grasped through the very apprehension of "this-ness" (*idantā*), the specific feature required for the difference is also manifested; thus, one must admit that the act of apprehension possesses the capacity for discrimination (*vivecakatva*).

Likewise, recollection (*smaraṇa*) too is indeed discriminative. For it is impossible to define this "conceit of recollection" (*smaraṇābhimāna*), whose loss would cause recollection to be non-discriminative. To explain: is the conceit of recollection (1) recollection itself; or (2) something other than recollection; or (3) a property belonging to recollection; or (4) the apprehension of an object as qualified by a previous experience; or (5) some particularity residing in recollection itself; or (6) a distinction caused by an object of knowledge distinct from the domain of the previous experience; or (7) the capacity to produce a difference in the result; or (8) the experience "I remember"?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because if memory were lost, it would follow that the cognition of silver itself does not exist. The second is not tenable, because if something else were lost, there would be the fallacy of a mismatch between subject and predicate (vaiyadhikaraṇya), since memory would then lack the capacity for non-discrimination. The third is not tenable, because no such property is perceived. Nor is the fourth tenable, because in the error of recognition—such as "This very Devadatta whom I saw before is this one"—one observes non-discrimination even while there is a grasp of the connection with the previous experience, and without any loss of that [experience].

Now, if it is argued that while this was said with reference to mere memory (*smṛti*), recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not like that, even so, this position is not tenable. To explain: does the prior experience take itself as its object, or only the object? Not the first, because it would involve a contradiction of the function [of consciousness]. In the second case, however, it is the object that is manifested by the memory, but not the prior cognition, because that was not experienced. If it is objected that in the case of "the jar is known," we observe a memory of the object qualified by cognition, we say no; for...

Because it is a distinct recollection. This recollection—produced either by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) or by an inference concerning the object of knowledge—is different from the recollection produced by the initial determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*), which has as its object the jar alone. Furthermore, by this [recollection] also, the prior experience called the "reflective awareness" which is its own producer is not made an object; rather, it is the jar itself, qualified by the determinative cognition, that is experienced through the reflective awareness.

Therefore, this is established: the memory under dispute does not apprehend an object qualified by the cognition that is its own source, because it is a memory, like the memory of word-meanings. For words generate a memory regarding the objects with which they are connected.

But surely the Buddhist does not tolerate this. For instance: since relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between words and their meanings are impossible, it is incorrect to say that [words] cause the recollection of related objects. If it is argued that the relation is the power to produce cognition, is that the power to produce experience (*anubhava*) or the power to produce recollection (*smṛti*)? Not the first, because although words in the form of a sentence produce the experience of the sentence-meaning, that [power] is absent with respect to their own individual referents.

At the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), because the meanings of words are apprehended through other means of knowledge, they lack the quality of being a "new object" (*apūrvārtha*). As it has been said: "A word is not distinguished from a mere reminder, because there is no additional [information] [conveyed by it]."

In the second case as well, that capacity does not produce remembrance while it remains unknown, because [remembrance] has cognition as its cause. Nor does it do so when it is known, because since capacity is to be understood solely through its effect, there would be a circularity between the production of remembrance and the cognition of capacity. Now, it might be argued: "By means of the activity of the middle-aged elder, one infers a cognition that is the cause of that activity; then, determining that the word is the producer of that [cognition] because it immediately precedes it, one ascertains the capacity at the very time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) through the methods of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpoddhāra*). Thus, there is no mutual dependence."

Even then, is the determination of the expressive power (śakti) with respect to the word alone, or with respect to that which is connected to a specific meaning? Not the first, because it would result in the impossibility of establishing the restriction that "this is the meaning of this word. As for the second, another relationship would have to be postulated to establish the connection of the expressive power, leading to an infinite regress.

If it is argued that the capacity (śakti) is self-explanatory as well as explanatory of others, even so, at the time of recollection, is the object remembered from the mere perception of the word? Or from the perception of the word possessing a capacity directed toward the object? Or from both the perception of the word and the mental impression (saṃskāra) produced by the knowledge of the capacity? Not the first, because it would lead to a lack of restriction (aniyama). Not the second, because since the object would have been perceived at the very moment of perceiving the word, a memory produced by the word would be redundant. Not the third, because memory cannot arise from that alone.

In other cases, there is a restriction based on other relations such as similarity, opposition, or the relation of cause and effect between the rememberer and the remembered; however, since such [relations] do not exist between a word and its meaning, words are merely remembrancers, whereas the sentence is the means of valid cognition—this is merely a formal procedure of those who maintain the Veda.

To this it is replied: there is no fault whatsoever in the recollection of an object resulting from the perception of a word and the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of its capacity (*śakti*). What was stated previously—that "it is as elsewhere," and so forth—is incorrect. Is it being argued that, just as in other cases, similarity (*sādṛśya*) and the like must be admitted in the case of the word? Or is it being argued that, just as with the word, let there be only the capacity in other cases as well, and let there be no similarity and the like? Or is it being argued that, because of the absence of a fundamental relationship based on similarity and the like, the word does not produce recollection even though the capacity exists?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because no similarity is observed in the word, and there is the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating what has not been perceived; furthermore, since it is observed elsewhere, it need not be postulated here. The second is not tenable, because it is impossible to deny that which is being experienced. The third is not tenable, because it would entail a contradiction if a potent entity were to fail to produce its effect. Therefore, words possessing potency indeed generate recollection (*smṛti*) regarding objects. For in that case, previous experiences of the objects together with the words are not remembered.

Otherwise, just as in the case of jars and other things, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that even the experiences themselves would constitute the meanings of those respective words.

Nor is the fifth [alternative] tenable, because no distinction whatsoever is perceived among the intrinsic natures of cognitions apart from adventitious conditions such as their causes, objects, and so forth. Nor are the sixth and seventh [alternatives] possible, because there is an absence in memory of any object or result distinct from those belonging to the original experience. Nor is the eighth [alternative] valid; for while it might be argued that the experience "I remember" is non-discriminative here due to some kind of lapse (*pramoṣa*), only after its discriminative nature has been established elsewhere. But that very point remains unproven.

For this experience arises as permeated by words expressive of recollection, having abandoned words expressive of apprehension. How could this occur initially if there were no distinction between apprehension and recollection? Thus, there would be a circular dependency: the distinction existing only when there is experience, and experience existing only when there is the distinction. Therefore, since it is difficult to maintain that the conceit of recollection is what is being obscured, it follows that recollection itself possesses the power of discrimination.

If it is argued: "Since perception and recollection would both have the object alone as their domain, there would be no distinction between them; therefore, you too must necessarily admit that recollection has as its object the thing qualified by the previous experience—let that itself be the 'pride of recollection' (smaraṇābhimāna)," we say: No, for the distinction is established solely from the difference in their causes. Otherwise, even in your own view, what would be the difference between recollection and an inferential cognition whose object was previously experienced? The object would be the same in both cases.

If it is argued that memory is distinguished from the inference of cognition by the form "that" (*sa*), what is this form "that"? Is it the state of being qualified by remote space, time, and so forth; or is it the state of being mixed with a prior experience; or is it the state of being produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that inferences and the like would also possess the nature of memory. It cannot be the second, because it would follow that even the inference of cognition would possess it. As for the third, the cause of distinction would simply be the specific cause itself.

If it is argued that, in the case at hand as well, the recollection of silver is produced solely by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), we say no; for this has already been answered by the fact that the silver appears as being situated in front [of the observer]. Nor can it be maintained that its being situated in front is caused by non-discrimination (*aviveka*), because non-discrimination is not a causal factor with respect to error (*bhrama*).

For instance: is it the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between two things being perceived? Or is it between a thing being perceived and one being remembered? Or is it between two things both being remembered? In the latter case, since there would be an absence of both [perception and memory], the non-discrimination that causes error would also be absent, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that no error could occur. Not the second [option], because even in a dream, if there were non-discrimination between the self, which is being perceived, and blue or other objects, which are being remembered, it would follow that there would be the appearance "I am blue. As for the third [option], everything appearing in an illusion would appear as purely indirect (*parokṣa*), because everything [involved] would be something being remembered.

This being the case, one must recognize that in the inference of the memory-nature of the present cognition of silver standing before one, "appearing as something remote" (parokṣāvabhāsitva) is the limiting condition (upādhi).

Furthermore, this is the counter-argument against the inference [of the validity] of the cognition as it is: "The cognitions under dispute are not in accordance with reality, because they are sublated, like the conventional usage of error. Therefore, abandoning the stubborn insistence on the twofold division of knowledge, one must accept a third kind of cognition: erroneous cognition.

[Objection: "In that case, let there be no *akhyāti* (non-apprehension); let there be *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension). For silver existing in another place and time is apprehended as having the nature of shell by a sense organ affected by a defect while in contact with the shell. Nor does this entail the apprehension of even what has never been experienced, because factors such as similarity act as the restrictive conditions. [Reply: This is incorrect. Is the "otherness" (*anyathātva*) located in the cognition, or in the result, or in the object? It cannot be the first, for the "otherness" in the cognition must be stated as follows: "The cognition having the form of silver takes the shell as its objective support (*ālambana*)."

In this regard, what is meant by the mother-of-pearl being the objective support (*ālambana*)? Is it that it imparts its own form to the cognition? Or is it that it is the object of the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) prompted by the cognition? Not the first, because it is impossible for the mother-of-pearl to impart its own form to a cognition that is already seized by the form of silver. Nor the second, because it would follow that a sword, spear, bow, or the like—which are objects of the worldly transactions prompted by the sight of a tiger and so forth—would have to be the objective support of the cognition of the tiger.

Nor can there be a change in the result, for no difference is observed in the nature of the manifestation—the result—whether it occurs in error or in right knowledge. How could there be a change even in the object itself? Is it the identity of the mother-of-pearl with silver, or its transformation into the form of silver? Even regarding the first case, is there absolute difference between the mother-of-pearl and the silver, or are they both different and non-different? Not the first, because a real identity is impossible between two absolutely distinct things; furthermore, you do not admit the theory of indeterminacy (*anirvacanīyatva*).

If identity with emptiness (*śūnyatādātmya*) were perceived, then since that [identity] could also occur in the case of quality and its possessor (*guṇaguṇin*), the status of [such cognitions] as erroneous would be unavoidable; for inherence (*samavāya*), which is established merely through conventional procedure, does not exceed [the nature of] identity. On the other hand, in the view of difference-and-identity (*bhedābheda*), there would be no error, just as in the cognition "this is a spotted cow. Furthermore, even in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*), there would be no sublation (of the illusion): "The cognition of silver under dispute is non-sublatable, because it is a cognition of transformation, like the cognition of curd as a transformation of milk. Consequently, the mother-of-pearl would not be seen again, just as the milk [is not seen after it has transformed].

Let it not be argued that, just as there is a return to the state of a bud upon the departure of the sun’s heat—the cause for the transformation of a lotus into its blooming form—so too, upon the departure of the defect which was the cause for the transformation into silver, there should be a return to the state of mother-of-pearl. This is not so; for there is no such cognition as "the mother-of-pearl was indeed silver," in the way that one might say "the bud was indeed in full bloom. Even if such a cognition were to occur in some manner, the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) is untenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even a person free from defects would perceive silver.

Indeed, it has never been observed that the very same milk transforms into the form of curds for one person while not doing so for another. Therefore, the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) is not well-established. Let it be, then, the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*): the silver under dispute is of the nature of cognition, because it is directly perceived even in the absence of sensory contact, just like cognition itself. But surely, according to the Buddhist view, minds and mental factors arise in dependence upon four kinds of causes? In that case, the arising of the form of silver cannot possibly result from the "auxiliary condition" (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), such as light, since that serves only as a cause for clarity [of perception].

Nor does it arise from the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), such as the eye and so forth, because that serves merely as the cause for the restriction of the object. Nor does it arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), namely a prior cognition, because we observe the emergence of a heterogeneous delusion of silver immediately after a heterogeneous cognition of a jar. Nor does it arise from an external object called the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), since the Vijñānavādin does not admit its existence. If it is asked how, then, the form of silver appears in consciousness, we reply: it is through the power of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

If it is argued that if the *saṃskāra* (mental impression) were also enduring, it would contradict the tenet that "everything is momentary," and that even if it were momentary, its being an object of cognition would undermine the doctrine of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), we say: no. For it is accepted that within the beginningless stream of consciousness, whenever a prior cognition of silver arose, that very [cognition] is what constitutes the *saṃskāra*. Although this *saṃskāra* is separated by many heterogeneous cognitions, it nevertheless produces another, homogeneous cognition of silver at some point.

Just as a rice seed produces another seed of its own kind through a series of effects such as multiple sprouts and so forth, it is exactly like that. Now, if you think that the subsequent seed does not arise from the preceding seed, but rather from the continuum of the sprout and other effects produced by the preceding seed, then in this case as well, let the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) reside in the very continuum of cognitions produced by the prior cognition of silver. In this way, even the prior cognition of silver arises from a prior cognition of silver.
Therefore, silver—which is brought about by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is nothing but the form of cognition itself, yet it appears as if external due to delusion.

To this it is replied: Is that silver, being transcendental (*alaukika*), devoid of birth, or does it arise just like ordinary worldly silver? In the first case, it would not have the nature of a cognition that is being produced. In the second case as well, does it arise from an external object or from cognition? Not the first, because you do not admit the existence of external objects. Nor can pure cognition be the producer, since pure cognition is of the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*).

Now, even if silver is produced from a cognition generated by defective causes, does the very cognition that produces it apprehend the silver, or is it another cognition? It cannot be the former, because the producer and the produced are momentary and exist at different times, which would result in the impossibility of having a direct perception of silver. Nor can it be another cognition, for if that other cognition were not itself produced by non-defective causes, it could not apprehend the silver, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Even if [the cognition] were produced by a defective cause, if it were produced by silver, then since silver possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it would exist, and an external object would have to be admitted. However, if it is not produced by silver, then silver could not be its object; for it is accepted that an object is a cause that imparts its form to the cognition. Therefore, according to the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*), silver itself would not be perceived at all.

If it is objected: "Even for you, if the cognition of silver were a memory, it would be *akhyāti* (non-apprehension); if it were an apprehension, it would be *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) or *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension); for no other mode of cognition is possible besides memory and apprehension," we reply: not so. Is its impossibility due to the failure to identify a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or due to the failure to identify a distinct nature of the cognition itself, or due to the failure to identify a distinct object? It is not the first, because the causal complex consists of the conjunction (*saṃprayoga*), the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and the defect (*doṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that a defect (*doṣa*) is a cause only for the non-arising of an effect already previously obtained by way of being an obstacle, and not for the arising of a new effect; for non-arising, being of the nature of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), is beginningless and thus cannot be produced by a defect. Furthermore, defects such as wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*) are observed to produce entirely new effects. Nor can the defect be explained away (*anyathāsiddhi*) as merely an awakener of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), because such awakening is its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
For an axe, while performing the acts of raising and lowering, does not thereby fail to be the cause of the act of cutting.

If it is asked: "Since contact (saṃprayoga) is exhausted merely by producing the cognition of 'this-ness' (idantā), and since you do not admit memory (smṛti) here—even though a latent impression (saṃskāra) is the cause of memory—and since a defect (doṣa) is never seen to be an independent cause of cognition, how can there be the appearance of silver? It is replied: First, an internal organ modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) having as its object merely 'this-ness' is produced by the sense organ conjoined with a defect. Then, consciousness (caitanya) is manifested in that 'this-ness' and in the modification that grasps it; and ignorance (avidyā) resides within that consciousness.

Due to the influence of a defect (*doṣa*), [the mind] becomes agitated. In this context, the ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in consciousness delimited by a portion [of the object], being thus agitated, undergoes a transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of silver through the assistance of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of silver awakened by similarity. However, the ignorance residing in consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*), aided by the latent impression of the modification that grasped the silver, undergoes a transformation into the form of that modification. Both of these—the transformation into silver and the transformation into the modification—are illuminated by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which is their respective substrate; in this manner, there is the appearance of silver.

Although there are two cognitions here—an internal organ modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) and an ignorance modification (*avidyāvṛtti*)—nevertheless, their object is the unity attained through the mutual identity of the real and the unreal, namely the "this" and the "silver. Consequently, because the resulting fruit is delimited by that single object, the oneness of the cognition is also figuratively attributed [to it]. Nor do the second and third [alternatives] hold, because false cognition and its false object have already been defined.

Although in this case both sensory contact (*saṃprayoga*) and mental impression (*saṃskāra*) are individually capable of producing valid cognition and recollection respectively, nevertheless, since activity is impossible based merely on the continuous production of valid cognition and recollection, one must postulate a single false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) produced by both sensory contact and mental impression.

This is just as, even though the cognitions of individual phonemes arise in immediate succession, you yourself must postulate that the cognition of the final phoneme—conjoined with the impressions of the preceding phonemes—is the sole cause of the cognition of word-meaning, because such cognition could not otherwise be explained due to the absence of simultaneity among the phoneme-cognitions.
